notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg0284.tlg056.perseus-: Section 1.1.2.3: the separation in the Third Philippic quotation is given as 'What, then, is this?' after 'what is worst… is best for the future'; the treatise's quotation is compressed. In 1.1.1.5 the construction 'either… or [the course] which has considered' is elliptical; the second alternative seems to be the safe course, and the sentence may be corrupt. 'Pylaea' is the Amphictyonic assembly at Thermopylae.

2.5: 'ἔστω δὲ ὁ λόγος εἰς τὰ τῆς γνώμης ἔτι' seems corrupt; rendered tentatively. 2.7: 'νῦν τὰ μᾶλλον προτετιμημένα εὑρήσεις' reads like an intruded gloss within the quotation. 3.4: the final example breaks off ('the other said') with the alternative wording missing; the contrasted wordings earlier in the line are implied rather than stated. 3.5: Arthmius (Ἀρίθμιος in the text) is the usual reading; bracketed [ἂν] treated as deleted.

Line 1: the bracketed [τοῦ] is an editorial deletion and is left untranslated. Line 10: 'λίαν ὀλίγωροι' ('too negligent') is abrupt and its connection is unclear; possibly a fragment of the quotation. Line 13: [τι] is bracketed in the edition; translated without it. Line 12: 'τὸ ἐν γένει' bracketed in the edition after 'κατʼ εἶδος' omitted as a deletion.

In the first passage the phrase 'κατὰ τὸ ἐναντίον τοῦ ἀκολούθου' and the structure of the Meidias example are compressed; the rendering follows the evident sense. 'ὑπόστασις' is rendered 'consequential clause' (a clause suspended by τοιαῦτα/τοσαύτην/οὕτω and completed by ὥστε). In the Leptines passage on Conon, 'προσηγάγετο' appears to be corrupt; translated by sense as 'brought in'. 'μάλιστα δὲ τὸ γένος ποιεῖ' is obscure; rendered tentatively.

In the third passage, 'ἐπανελθὼν' ('coming back') appears to be truncated from the quoted Demosthenes passage, where it means returning home near death; '[near death]' is supplied. The phrase 'νῦν τὸ συλληπτικὸν εἰς ἐπίτασιν ὁμολογούμενον' is obscure and possibly corrupt; the rendering 'the summing-up, agreed upon for intensification' is tentative. The sentence 'ὡς δὲ ἤδη παρακολουθοῦντί σοι … παρέδειξα' is awkwardly constructed and its rendering is uncertain. The final quotation ('and if you know me to be such a man...') is cut short and its connection to the point is unclear.

Line 1.4.1.10: 'ὃ μὲν διοικεῖται ἐστίν' is awkward and possibly corrupt; rendered by sense. Line 1.4.1.12: bracketed [εἶτα] and [καὶ] are editorial deletions; 'χθὲς μὲν οὖν' rendered 'or rather yesterday'. Line 1.4.2.3: συνδρομή (concurrence, i.e. agreeing with an anticipated objection) is a rare technical term; the quoted words 'καὶ μάλα ὀρθῶς δοκεῖ' are taken as the concession. Line 1.5.1.2: 'ἐκνενευρισμένοι χρήματα καὶ συμμάχους' quotes Demosthenes in abbreviated form; 'stripped of' supplied by sense.

1.5.1.5: the last sentence is elliptical in the Greek ('the most important thing to know is that when...'); translated as transmitted. 1.5.3.2: 'πάντα ἐξαίρει' does not construe; probably read 'πάντα <τὰ> ἐξαίροντα' ('all things that heighten'), translated so. 1.6.1.1: in the Leptines quotation 'took forty-nine triremes captive' renders 'fifty less one'. 1.6.2.1: the Aristolochus quotation is compressed and partly unclear ('now many [own it]'). 1.7.1.2: the passage paraphrasing and quoting Demosthenes, On the False Embassy, is confused in places, especially 'πρότασις ἂν ἔδοξεν εἶναι...μετατεθειμένος', which appears corrupt or lacunose; the sense supplied in brackets is conjectural.

In 1.10.1.2 ἐπιστροφαί is taken as 'recapitulations' (returns to the point); the sense is uncertain. 1.10.1.3: the bracketed words are a scholiast's gloss kept in brackets by the edition. 1.12.2.2 'Fittingly he is bound by certain [restraints]' (ἐνέχεταί τισιν) is obscure and possibly corrupt. 1.12.2.3 is confused, especially the comparison of deliberative and judicial lengths and the sentence beginning τοῦτο δὲ σημεῖον; the subject of βούλεται is unexpressed, rendered '[the art]'. 1.12.2.4: the final clause (ὡς μὴ…) is rendered literally, though the sense required seems to be 'so that the whole speech is consistent with itself'. 1.12.2.5: the bracketed [προσαναγκάζεσθαι] is the edition's deletion; the clause on 'the honourable' (ὑπάρχοι δʼ ἂν εἰ…) seems corrupt.

Line 2 'in the common things': sense uncertain (perhaps 'in what concerns the public'). In the 'boar' example the Greek infinitive construction is ambiguous between subject and object; the bracket gives the alternative reading the example turns on. Line 12 begins abruptly and seems unrelated to its context; it may be misplaced. In the final passage the train of argument (who 'they' are in 'harm to them', 'benefits to them') is loose and the text may be corrupt.

Line 1.14.1: '[τὰ δὲ]' is bracketed in the edition and left untranslated; the paraphrase is of Iliad 1.1–42. Line 1.14.2 paraphrases Odyssey 9.425–436. Line 2.2.1.1.1: ἐννοήματα 'περὶ τὴν ἑρμηνείαν' is awkward; the sense seems to be 'thoughts used in exposition'.

Line 1: 'τὸ κατὰ τὰς ἀποβάσεις λέγειν οὐ πολιτικώτερον' is obscure and probably corrupt; rendered literally. Line 2: the quoted Xenophon has 'ἕτερα δὲ καινὰ δαιμόνια εἰσφέρων· ἀδικεῖ δὲ καὶ' in line 10, here abbreviated in the edition to 'ἕτερα δὲ καὶ τοὺς νέους διαφθείρων'; the Xenophon text has been supplied in translation for sense. Line 8: 'ὅσα δὲ ἐπεὶ ἐπʼ ἀνδράσιν ἐγένετο' is a garbled quotation (Agesilaus 1.6); rendered tentatively. Line 11: 'διάθεοις' read as διάθεσις.

Line 1: 'πρὸς τὰ προσόντα τῷ' appears defective (a noun seems lost after τῷ); rendered 'the qualities that belonged to [the man]'. The bracketed [πρῶτον μὲν] is the edition's. In Line 9 the sentence 'Ξενοφῶντος δὲ ἦθος καὶ ἡ χεὶρ αὐτῷ ἐπηκολούθησεν' is obscure and probably corrupt (perhaps 'and his hand followed' refers to the Chaerephon passage, where Socrates' brother story involves hands); rendered literally. In Line 10 the Chaerephon anecdote is in fact about Chaerecrates quarrelling with Chaerephon; the author's attribution is kept.

Line 1: ἵνα ἄλλον is odd; probably read ἄλλον τινά or similar, rendered 'another person'. Line 6: [ἐπεμελεῖτο] is bracketed in the edition; the sentence is compressed and the sense uncertain. Line 7: 'from the necessary to the necessary' is likely corrupt (perhaps a negative or different term lost). Line 10: σπουδάρχαις is odd and possibly corrupt; the example of Critias is also obscure. Line 11: 'upright' and 'oblique' refer to the nominative/finite construction versus a participial one.

περιβολή rendered 'amplitude' (Hermogenean idea); added to glossary. In 2.5.1.4 ὀρθοῦν/πλαγιάζειν taken as nominative vs oblique (genitive absolute) constructions. In 2.8.1.4 the bracketed [γνωρίσεως] appears to be an editorial deletion and is not translated. In 2.6.1.3 the dog quotation lacks a predicate ('good' supplied).

Line 1: the edition punctuates the first sentence as a question; 'δυνάμει' may be suspect after a discussion of truthfulness. Line 3: the final clause (τὸ πῶς ἂν γένοιτο οὐδὲν ἄλλως ἔχοι) is syntactically doubtful and probably corrupt; rendered literally. Line 10: ἐτιμελείᾳ read as ἐπιμελείᾳ. Line 16: the closing clause (τὸ πόθεν γίνεται ἀξίωμα πρᾷόν τι εἶναι) is obscure and possibly corrupt; the rendering is tentative. Line 19: ἀνεικός is not a recognised form; read as something like ἀνειμένον/ἀφελῆ ποιοῦν ('makes unforced'), tentatively.

Line 4.1: 'με ταύτης' is evidently corrupt; translated as 'with her' (cf. Xenophon, Cyropaedia, συνανέστησαν αὐτῇ). Line 5.1: 'κινδυνεύει' clause and 'ὁ δὲ' are somewhat awkward but the sense is clear. Line 13.1: the contrast of 'demonstratives' with 'ἐξεταστικά' (here 'inquiring forms') is obscure, and the example given seems to illustrate a demonstrative, so the passage may be defective; the Philammon quotation (Demosthenes, On the Crown 319) is truncated, and the bracketed words supply its sense. Line 16.1: 'συγγραφικὸν δὲ εἰ δεῖ τελείου λόγου' appears corrupt; translated tentatively. The bracketed sentence at the start of 16.1 is bracketed by the edition.

Line 1: συμπολοκαί read as συμπλοκαί ('connections', i.e. linking by conjunctions). Line 2: ἐπίσταται read as ἐφίσταται ('appears suddenly'); the point about κόψας / κρούσας (two verbs for knocking) is obscure in the text. Line 5: κίρνησιν read as κιρνάς; χητήσῃ as ζητήσῃ; ὑπὸ τῶν probably for ὑπὸ τίνων ('under what'). The quotation 'about skill' renders σοφίας.

In line 25 the phrase 'care is rather produced' (ἐπιμέλεια μᾶλλον γίνεται) is obscure, and the sentence may be corrupt. Line 27: Xenophon, Symposium 1.4; 'cleansed out' renders ἐκκεκαθαρμένοις. 'Not pure' (οὐ καθαρὰν) seems to mean that the trope is not undiluted or bold; the reading is uncertain. In line 28, 'memoirs' renders ἀπομνημονεύμασιν (perhaps Xenophon's Memorabilia).

nodes.text: On Political Speech

Here, for you, is [an account] of the forms and virtues from which political speech is composed, by which it is tested, and through which it is advanced as worth much, being put together, as it were, from parts, each one by one, complete on every side and holding itself perfectly within itself. These [forms] are of this kind and this number: solemnity, gravity, amplitude, credibility, vehemence, emphasis, forcefulness, care, sweetness, clarity and purity, brevity and concision, restraint.
On solemnity.

Solemnity, then, is in general constituted in three ways: in thought, in figure, and in expression. By thought I mean the sense and the conceptions in which the subject matter is found; by figures, the shape of the speech, in which the thoughts, as they are brought out, make the speech appear either of this kind or of that. And these have the greatest power in speech, as much as living and moving things have over things in the opposite condition. By expression I mean the diction itself, through which the conceptions are expressed.

In thought, then, your speech will be solemn from conceptions already held in honour. In a word, things are 'held in honour' when one uses glorious matters, and something is said about glorious things, and whatever is rare and ancient. Glorious, first of all, are the things of the gods, as when you lead your ideas back to divine things, the goodwill of the gods, the kindness of fortune, as in: 'in many cases, it seems to me, one might see the goodwill that comes from the gods', and anything of that sort.

And among human things too, when you lead [the speech] to what is held in honour: honouring parents, ancestors, those who first established the customs, and when you urge the same on others; and in general the things held in honour in life also share in solemnity, such as freedom, self-control, justice, as when you call freedom, and what is produced from it, the boundary and rule of happiness. And in general one could name countless things of this kind, which are plain to all who have once entered into this study.

Things of this kind also share in solemnity: when you discourse about life and death, as in 'for death is the end of life for all men'; or when you speak and divide and define natures, as in 'for there is no race of friends and of enemies'.

In these lies the greatest danger in political speech: either that, following and being drawn along by the nature of the conceptions, and departing altogether from the matters at hand, one ruins the credit of the speech and makes it hollow, and becomes like those sophists who discourse on things on high; or [the course] which has considered the measure in these matters, how far the speech of contest may be raised, and with what things it may be mixed without failing to keep its solemnity within the bounds of contest and without going astray. These matters, then, [belong] to those who are being instructed.

Now let us return to the things from which the less hazardous solemnity is constituted. These are glorious deeds and designs, and the rarest and most extraordinary of exploits, such as Xerxes conceiving the plan to bridge the Hellespont, and to dig through Athos and sail [through it]; and the Athenians enduring to abandon their city and go aboard their ships; and the Spartans shutting the gates against the king. For these are great deeds and designs of solemnity, and naturally these too raise the speech to solemnity.

For the sake of example, let there be a thought that in itself, from its conception, partakes of solemnity: 'No, by those of our ancestors who faced danger in the front line at Marathon, and those who stood in battle order at Plataea.' For here the question was whether the city rightly or wrongly took the risk at Chaeronea, whether choosing this war was a mistake or not. This is the question, and the proof has become: it was not a mistake, because neither did the ancestors who faced danger in the front line at Marathon make a mistake. But to swear by the ancestors as though by gods: this holds the height of solemnity, 'No, by those of our ancestors who faced danger in the front line at Marathon.' It is clear that the right occasion for such conceptions is in glorious contests and those of the highest importance, not when we prosecute someone, or are prosecuted, for damage or some other of the most trivial matters. One might also say that the whole is a figure of an oath; for the very phrase 'No, by those who faced danger in the front line at Marathon' is not an oath but an example, as in: 'you did not make a mistake in taking up the danger for the freedom and safety of all, just as neither did those who faced danger in the front line at Marathon'; for facing danger in the front line at Marathon is like taking up the danger for the safety of all. So he shaped the matter into an example instead of saying it directly, and at the same time, for brilliance and credibility, turned it into the semblance of an oath.

Speaking of ancient things also belongs to solemnity, as in: 'considering that Orestes, having killed his mother, met with gods as kindly judges and was acquitted.' In thought, then, solemnity might arise in this way.

In figure, as follows: when one uses declarative figures, as Demosthenes in the speech Against Aristogeiton: 'the whole life of men, whether they live in a small city or a large one, is governed by nature and by laws.'

Or when one uses detachments. The nature of the figure of detachment is something like this: when, departing from weaving [the thoughts] together in sequence and attaching them to one another, we go back to a fresh beginning, so that the connection of the conceptions is separated and detached. As in the Philippics, in the speech Against Philip: the proposition being established is 'Philip is doing terrible things; for he does this and that', for instance: 'he has enslaved Thessaly, the cities in Euboea are already under tyrants, he has gone off to the Hellespont, earlier he came against Ambracia, he holds Elis, so great a city in the Peloponnese.' And the amplifying [part], 'and while he does such things none of the Greeks stops him', in which he says: 'and knowing this, we Greeks do not send envoys about these things and show our anger'; at the end, 'so that, while he acts, what are we ourselves doing?' And the amplification by contrast: 'and this, when our ancestors yielded none of these things, not only to the barbarians, but not even to the most glorious of the Greeks, not to the Spartans, not to the Athenians, not lastly to the Thebans.' Then the statement of cause on top of all: 'What, then, is the cause of these things?' Here now pay attention to the figure of detachment; for I went through everything beforehand for the sake of clarity for you. If he had wished to bring out the confirming thought by weaving it together, he would have done it thus: 'because they all hated those who took money from men wishing to rule or to corrupt Greece.' But he did not do so; instead, breaking off the weaving together of the thoughts and detaching it from being joined to itself, he leads back to a beginning and says: 'There was something then, there was, men of Athens, in the minds of the many. What was this? They all hated those who took money from men wishing to rule or to corrupt Greece.' So it became something different in figure, even though it is one and the same conception, whether I say it woven together, 'What, then, is the cause of these things? That they did not think thus', or whether, using detachment, I lead back: 'There was something then, there was, in the minds of the many.' And elsewhere, using an announcement: 'I shall speak with frankness; for indeed I could not do otherwise', then, detaching, he adds: 'all the generals who have ever sailed out from you'. These too are figures of detachment: 'A fine thing, men of Athens, a fine thing is the guarding of public affairs', and its opposite: 'A foul thing, men of Athens, a foul thing is the beast, and unsociable.' It is not because countless other devices are not present in each of these examples that I did not mention them one by one; for indeed in some of them there is also reduplication, and [the thought] is expressed universally, not in part; but our task is to point out each of the generic figures one at a time, and you too asked for it so. And in general several devices often coincide in a single thought, especially those of the same kinship, and the speech takes on those from which it is perfectly constructed in all its parts: thought, figure, rhythm, diction. But our discussion now concerns figure alone, and that only the figure of thought. There are also other detachments, as: 'Meidias will suffer nothing terrible or pitiable if he comes to possess as much as the many among you', and again: 'many rich men banded together, having gained the reputation of being somebody through their wealth', and again: 'Meidias perhaps hates me.'

Separations also have solemnity, as when he says: 'What, then, is he attempting? To make war on the Amphictyons and turmoil about the Pylaea.' For without the separation it would be like this: 'For Philip thought that, if he were to persuade either the Thessalians or the Thebans to march against you for the sake of his own enmity, no one would pay attention to him, but if he took up their common grievances and were chosen leader, he hoped more easily to deceive them in some things, and in others by whatever means. What then? He makes war on the Amphictyons and turmoil about the Pylaea.' That, without the separation, would have been confused and low; but what raises it to solemnity is the separation in between, 'What, then, is he attempting?', and then the matter after the separation, 'to make war on the Amphictyons'. And elsewhere: 'what is worst in the past, this is best for the future.' Here too, without the separation, it would have been to add at once: 'for we do none of what is needed.' Where, then, is the separation? In the middle part, in which, separating, he says: 'What, then, is this? That we do none of what is needed.' But these divisions arise from the matter, 'What, then, is he attempting?' or again 'What, then, is this?'; those others come from some judgement of his own, as when he says: 'for indeed so it is, I was outraged and my body was then treated with contempt.' And making the speech distinct always accompanies separation, and in places making it clear as well. One must know that the devices of speech draw much beauty after them; but we are now concerned with one, the most generic.

It is also a figure of solemnity when one uses oblique constructions. For where the thoughts are put in the direct case, the speech is chopped up into single pieces, and the figure belongs to the purer style rather than to the more solemn. For this reason in the speech Against Leptines, as long as Demosthenes [puts] the thoughts directly, the speech seems pure, as: 'The Thirty are said to have borrowed money from the Lacedaemonians against those in the Piraeus.' Another thought in the same style: 'When those affairs were settled, the Lacedaemonians sent envoys and demanded the money back.' And if he had carried on what follows in the same style, directly, he would have said: 'So there were discussions, and some thought that those from the city should repay the money, others that those from the Piraeus should'; but the tension of the figure and the solemnity would have been destroyed. For this reason he puts it obliquely and says: 'Discussions taking place, and some urging that those from the city should repay, others those in the Piraeus, this was the first sign of concord.' And at the beginning of the speech Against Philip: 'Many speeches, men of Athens, being made about the wrongs Philip commits.' And something else put obliquely after this: 'and all, I know well, would say so.' And again: 'The present affairs being, men of Athens, fearful for everyone, as I judge, no one of all is in greater danger than you.'

This one must know first of the figures, that dignity and solemnity have a certain partnership in speech: for where the speech takes on dignity, there it also takes on solemnity. Let the discussion [turn] to matters of thought: further, using similes makes the speech have solemnity and dignity, as: 'like an unsettled wind at sea, moving as chance has it', and again: 'like a thunderbolt or a torrent this whole business fell upon the city', and again elsewhere: 'since no one is unaware that, like the recurrence or the onset of a fever or of some other ill, it comes even upon one who now seems to stand very far away.'
And making maxims also belongs to solemnity, as: 'for faring well beyond one's merit becomes for the foolish a starting point for thinking ill.'

And to throw out and do away with things less highly esteemed, and to bring in instead things more highly prized, belongs to solemnity: 'I did not fortify the city with stones or with bricks; but if you wish to learn of my fortification, you will now find the things more highly prized: arms, and cities, and places, and harbours.'

It also has solemnity when you do not at once run to the thing being introduced, but first take up its powers and hold the speech in suspense: 'One common safeguard the nature of sensible men possesses in itself'; and he did not at once add and say 'distrust', but having first taken up its powers and holding it in suspense, 'which is good and saving for all, but most of all for the masses against tyrants', and another resumption, 'What, then, is this?', then the thing introduced, 'distrust'. Similar to this is that other passage: 'what both overcame the wealth of the Persians and kept Greece free, and was defeated neither in sea battle nor in land battle, but now, having perished, has ruined everything and turned all affairs upside down'; and with so much set out beforehand, the 'what' has not yet been said, but using a resumption he will now introduce it: 'What, then, was this?' Then the thing introduced by itself, as 'distrust' there, so here: 'all hated those who took money from men wishing to rule or to corrupt Greece.'
And definitions put in universal terms have solemnity, as: 'for I consider the wealth of a city to be allies, trust, goodwill.'

And always to put forward reputable persons or matters, drawing [the point] away from oneself, is very solemn, as: 'and none of this is new, nor my invention, but the ancient law which this man transgressed commands that laws be made so', and again: 'speaking not words of my own, but the writings of your ancestors.'

This too is a figure of solemnity, to set the thoughts side by side without connectives, placing them one after another, as: 'Meidias of Anagyrus has been put forward; he knows the secrets; the city cannot contain him.' And again: 'He goes off to the Hellespont; earlier he came against Ambracia; he holds Elis, so great a city in the Peloponnese; he plotted against Megara lately; neither Greece nor the barbarian land can contain the man's greed.'

In expression, solemnity arises as follows: when one uses nominal words instead of verbal ones, as: 'A great advantage, men of Athens, belonged to Philip.' And: 'For irrational daring was considered comrade-loving courage.'

And when you use figurative words instead of proper ones, as calling bribery a disease: 'A disease, men of Athens, a terrible one, has fallen upon Greece.' And again elsewhere: 'then the man setting up this engine against the city.' And in the speech Against Meidias: 'but you, having made up the full contribution to such a club, are right to collect it from this man for yourself.'
And speaking in accumulation and setting the words one after another belongs to solemnity, as: 'fortunate, and great, and fearsome to all Greeks and barbarians.'

And to remove the persons and carry the speech forward upon the matters themselves is very solemn: 'if Thespiae and Plataea and the [prospect] that the Thebans would very soon pay the penalty had not taken away the truth'. [He might have said] 'but those saying the things about the Thespians and Plataeans', but he, removing the persons of the speakers, speaks of the things themselves on their own: 'if Thespiae and Plataea had not'. And elsewhere again: 'but I think it is not you who must be persuaded to keep the peace'; and he [would have] said the opposite, 'but Philip', but he, removing the person, spoke indefinitely about the matter: 'but the one who is pursuing the business of war'. And again elsewhere, wishing to show that Philip is the one making the war, instead of saying thus: 'but if Philip, holding arms in his hands and a great force around him', the other said.

It belongs to solemnity also to use words of a more generic kind; by generic I mean: gold, silver. For what comes from these is what is spoken of by species and part: money, means, revenue. But Thucydides, leading these back to the generic, produced solemnity; Hermocrates says of the Carthaginians: 'for they have very much gold and silver', instead of 'for they are very rich', or, changed another way, 'for they are rich'. And Demosthenes, instead of saying 'Arthmius was punished because he corrupted certain people with money in the Peloponnese', speaking generically, that he 'brought gold from the King', produced solemnity.

One must know that solemnity also arises from a single word, as in the speech Against Leptines, where he says that one must keep the stelae valid. How did he raise it to solemnity? By the last word: 'so that they may be a memorial of the city's character.'
On gravity.

Gravity arises in general in thought and in figure, but in expression hardly at all. In thought, gravity arises as follows: when one proceeds to accuse either oneself or one of one's relatives or friends; for such a thing would be grave, when it is possible to praise, or in general [to accuse] any of those on whose behalf one speaks or to whom one speaks, as Demosthenes: 'I have meddled, and the city that was persuaded by me has meddled; let all the errors and wrongs be mine.'

Where you can show to an exceptional degree that you do no wrong, there use such boldness as to deprive yourself of the pardon or kindness of the jurors, as when you say: 'Do not endure even my voice, not even if I have conducted all public affairs exceedingly well, but stand up and condemn me at once'; gravity arises here too. And in the case of a friend gravity likewise arises, if you deprive him of either the pardon or the kindness of the jurors. Gravity also arises when you call down something outrageous upon yourself, as: 'and yet I would rather be dead than have said these things.'

And when one puts forward to the hearers something outrageous which they would not willingly accept, as in the speech Against Aristogeiton, having gone through what happens in the assemblies through the inexperience of such orators, he put forward the outrageous thing with gravity: 'if then you want these things, and these men do them with our consent, one must go on one's way and let it be.'

And when you lead the argument to an absurdity, you produce gravity, as in the speech Against Callicles: 'for Callicles will surely not force me to drink it up'; or when you concede to the opponent things admittedly outrageous, as in the speech Against Aristogeiton: 'if Aristogeiton is simply wicked and bitter and a sycophant, I grant it, I concede, Philocrates, that you, being such, may save one like yourself.'

And when someone, having gone through everything, leaves one single thing to the opponent, as being in his favour no less than against him, gravity arises, as: 'except, by Zeus, there is this: he has a brother, the one who brought that fine suit against him.' And again, having removed the reasons why they ought not [to have done it], he adds: 'unless someone should say this: because we were mad; for there is nothing else to say.'

And when you bring illustrious dead men into the judgment, such a thing seems to be grave, as: 'and yet how loudly our ancestors would groan.' And again: 'and yet what anger, do you suppose, would your ancestors have felt, or what vote would they have cast, against those responsible for this ruin?'

It belongs to gravity also to leave aside, as things that will be said, what no one would say: 'We will tell the Greeks, by Zeus: "There is a law of Timocrates among us; so wait for the ninth *prytany* [term of the presiding council]; then we will march out."'
And conceding past outrages, as in 'up to this point, then, let the matter be settled by you', is gravity.

It belongs to gravity also to pray against outrageous things: 'and yet may affairs not come to this, men of Athens.' 'It is ten thousand times better to be dead than to do anything for Philip out of flattery.'

In figure, gravity arises in this way, when someone uses the figure of thought, as: 'Alike, are they not, Solon the lawgiver and Timocrates?' Or again: 'A fine reward the majority of the Oreites have received for entrusting themselves to Philip's friends and hating Euphraeus; a fine one too the people of Eretria, for driving away your envoys and giving themselves up to Cleitarchus; and indeed they are slaves, and are whipped.'

It belongs to gravity also to use the figures of indignation, as: 'Charidemus, alas!', and the phrase of Aeschines: 'you endured it utterly, like men of iron.' And aposiopeses will have the same force for you, as: 'what could one call you and address you rightly?'

Gravity also arises when you are led on to say something painful against the hearers, which one thinks they would take badly, and then you correct it as having nothing milder to say, as is also the case in the Letters: 'if you look upon the illustrious dignity of the Council or the Areopagus, remember the trial of Aristogeiton and cover your faces; for I have no gentler address to speak to those who have wronged me myself.'

This sort of thing also has gravity, when, having granted something as being so for you, you then remove it and cast doubt on it, as is also the case in the Philippics: 'but he, while you stay at home, are at leisure, are in good health' — having granted this as being so for them, he at once removed it, correcting himself: 'if indeed we should say that those who do such things are in good health.'
And the expressions of perplexity in indignant passages have gravity, as in the Letters: 'O — what could I say so as neither to seem to err nor to lie? Too negligent.'
On amplitude.

Amplitude arises, in general, by thought, by figure, by expression. By thought in this way: when someone adds indefinite things to definite ones, as: 'one could see his ingratitude and malice from many places' — this is the indefinite thing taken in from outside; now the definite: 'but not least from what he said about fortune.' And again: 'I am at a disadvantage in many respects in this contest against Aeschines.' This is indefinite; now the definite, taken in as a collection: 'but in two, men of Athens, and great ones'; then he divided these by species: 'one, that the contest is not now for equal stakes for me; the other, which is natural to all, to listen gladly to abuse and accusations, but to be vexed with those who praise themselves.' For all these belong to amplitude: the adding of the indefinite, 'I am at a disadvantage in many respects'; the gathering into a collection, 'but in two, men of Athens, and great ones'; the dividing by species, 'one, that the contest is not for equal stakes; the other, that all are so disposed as to listen gladly to those who abuse, but to be vexed with those who praise themselves.' And a third example: 'in many instances, men of Athens, one might, I think, see the goodwill of the gods made manifest to the city'; then the leading down to the definite: 'but not least in the present circumstances.' And again: 'many of the things done by him are worthy of praise, but greatest of all is the raising of the walls.'

This too is amplitude, when you set out the matters by genus and then go through them by species, as in the speech Against Leptines. What he wants to introduce is this: 'so one must consider not only that Leucon is not wronged, but also Epicerdes'; but before stating the species, 'but also Epicerdes', he anticipated with the genus: 'but also anyone else who did you good while he was prospering, and to whom receiving exemption from you has now become a need'; then he came to the species, setting it apart: 'Who then is this? Epicerdes of Cyrene.' And again, introducing the benefactions of Epicerdes, he anticipated with the genus and so introduced the species: 'but to one who, at such a moment, when even among those who had been well treated it was hard to find anyone willing to remember the benefits he had received.' Now he states what he did, by species: 'for this man gave a hundred minas to those of the citizens who had met misfortune in Sicily.' And again, by genus: 'buildings, and adornment of temples and harbours and of what goes with these, so great and of such a kind they left us that no room for surpassing them has been left to any of those who come after'; then by species: 'these Propylaea, the Parthenon, the ship-sheds.' And again in the speech Against Leptines, wishing to examine and discredit those who supported the law, he first mentioned them by genus: 'advocates have been chosen for the law, and especially men clever at speaking'; then by species: 'Leodamas of Acharnae and Cephisodotus of Kerameis'; then again, gathering them by genus: 'hear what might justly be replied to these'; then again by species: 'first, to Leodamas.' So when you do not speak by species alone, but anticipate with the genus, you produce amplitude.

It is also amplitude when someone, in the middle of a thought or thoughts, before completing the sense, inserts other thoughts; this, if it is not done with some measure, produces terrible obscurity. An example of this amplitude is in the speech Against Aristocrates: 'You would reasonably, men of Athens, both pay attention to me and hear with goodwill what I say'; then things establishing that they ought to listen attentively, one inserted upon another, and these in oblique construction: 'since, though I am not one of those who trouble you, nor of those engaged in politics among you, I claim I will show a matter of such importance to have been done, if you will contend alongside me as far as is in you and listen eagerly.' And not one good, but two, will result for them from listening: one from the present, 'you will both preserve this', the other from the future, 'and you will make [men] not hold back, if any of us too thinks he can do the city some good.' This then is complete and lacks nothing; but he, so that the amplitude might become greater, set beside it the opposite as well and resumed. And what was the opposite of someone being more eager to do the city some good? 'But as it is, many, fearing this — not clever at speaking, perhaps, but nonetheless better men than the clever — do not even think of considering any public matter.' And this would have been complete; but even here he was not satisfied, but added a confirmation to what had been said, drawn from his own case: 'I at any rate, be well assured, would myself have shrunk from bringing this indictment', so that in this way the paying of attention to the speaker has been woven together. And this will not be absurd, that some shrink from doing the city good, as they now do shrink, through fear and inexperience in speaking: 'I at any rate nearly shrank myself.' How then do you accuse? And the confirmation of this too is from his own case: 'because I think it terrible that formerly, when I sailed as trierarch to the Hellespont, I spoke and accused certain men whom I thought were wronging you, but now should keep quiet and be silent when I see certain people contriving a matter unprofitable to the city.' Do the thoughts inserted seem few to you, before the whole idea comes to its close in this?

And so that it may become still clearer to you what sort of thing it is to insert several thoughts in the middle, that is a very clear example in the speech On the False Embassy: 'for, with a mortal man' — one thought, from the person — 'and one powerful through certain circumstances, to write and conclude an immortal peace' — the shame against the city, the act being done; and what follows it, and it is not yet complete, but he inserts more. Again: 'for how is it not shameful that publicly all of you censure what was done as a result of the peace, and are unwilling to take part in the proceedings among the Amphictyons, and are ill-disposed and suspicious towards Philip, as though what was done were impious and terrible, and neither just nor advantageous to you; but, having come into the court' — now attend to the insertions — 'to judge the accounting for these things' — another thought — 'having sworn an oath on behalf of the city' — 'the man whom you have caught in the act of having done such things' — now what completes it — 'to acquit this man?'

Amplitude is also produced when one does not examine only what follows from the matter, but also takes in the opposites, as in the speech On the False Embassy. The simple and consequent [statement] would have run thus: 'for since you elected this man ambassador, to guard the others'; here, taking in the opposite, he brings in the consequent thus: 'you elected this man' — first what he was not going to do, then what he was going to do — 'not as one of those who would sell what is yours, nor as one of those who had put their trust in Philip' — then now the consequent — 'but to guard the others.' And again in the speech On the False Embassy: 'when the assembly came, Aeschines came forward first of us all', and he did not at once bring in the consequent, 'he reported the following', but first, by the opposite of the consequent, what he ought to have reported and did not report. And what were these things? First: 'from reporting anything about the matters of the embassy, or about what had been said in the Council, in case he disputed that I was telling the truth, he refrained altogether'; then now, according to the consequent, what he did and said in the assembly: 'and he spoke such words.' And so that you may know that the principles of amplitude are akin to one another: we said above that amplitude is to anticipate with the genus and bring in the species; but now let us also say that amplitude is not only to examine what follows, but also the opposites of what follows. Here he has done both: what he did not do and what he did, setting the opposite before the consequent; and anticipating with the genus before the species, stating the genus in 'and he spoke such words, containing benefits so great and of such a kind that he went off having won all of you over.' This is by genus; now the species: 'for he said he had come having persuaded Philip'; then again by genus: 'of everything that is advantageous to the city'; then by species: 'both about the affairs among the Amphictyons and about all the rest.' And in the speech Against Meidias: 'as one must, if anyone has been outraged by this man,' — the consequent — 'claim to obtain justice', and the opposite of the consequent — 'and not keep silent.'

It belongs to amplitude also not to introduce the thoughts, that is, the facts, bare, but to take in beforehand the opinion about such things, or the quality of the opinion. Thus he produced amplitude: 'the Lacedaemonians seem to me to be doing the work of very clever men'; then what was being done by them: 'for now they say that the Eleans ought to recover part of Triphylia.' And in the Philippics: 'and you would, I think, deliberate much better about the war and the whole preparation'; then he adds that for whose sake these things were said beforehand: 'if you were to consider, men of Athens, the position of the country against which you are making war.'

You also produce amplitude when, before stating what is being introduced, you anticipate what confirms it. For instance in the speech Against Leptines: if he had spoken simply and without amplitude, he would have said thus: 'and while some bade [them] repay those from the city, and others to settle jointly'; but as it is, see how he anticipated the confirming points for each side. He did not at once say 'some ... those from the city', but in between, 'bidding the borrowers repay those from the city'; and 'others' — and he did not at once set against it 'to settle jointly', but again anticipated the confirmation: 'while others thought it right that this should first be the token [of concord], to settle the debts jointly.'

This too belongs to amplitude, when you do not state what is introduced bare. For instance in the speech Against Leptines, what was being introduced was: 'this being in the valid laws, that all the gifts which the people gave should be valid'; but he anticipated the quality of what was being introduced: 'this being in the laws that are valid' — then the quality taken in — 'a fine thing, men of Athens, and clear' — and now what is being introduced — 'that all the gifts which the people gave should be valid.' And again, after it, the judgement: 'just, O earth and gods!' And generally, wherever you do not introduce the facts bare, but anticipate something about them or add something to them, you will produce amplitude.

You also produce amplitude when, introducing something of your own, for instance 'Conon did you so many services', you do not say at once what he did, but anticipate from what [resources] he did what, and in what circumstances he did it, as in the speech Against Leptines. The benefaction was 'he defeated [them] at sea'; but before saying this, he anticipated and brought in also in what circumstances he did what: 'after the return of the people from Piraeus, when our city was weak and possessed not a single ship, serving as general for the King, and having received from us no resources whatever' — now what was done by him — 'he defeated the Lacedaemonians at sea.'

By figure, amplitude comes about thus. The figure by supposition especially produces amplitude, and also when one uses consequential clauses. What consequential clauses in speech are and how much they can do, you will learn from examples, as in the speech Against Conon, right at the beginning: 'having been outraged, men of the jury, and having suffered at the hands of this Conon here'. The simple way would have been to say thus: 'many terrible things', or 'various things, than which nothing more terrible has happened'; but he produced amplitude through the consequential clause: 'such things that for a very long time neither my family nor any of the doctors expected me to survive.' The distinctive feature of the consequential clause also matters somewhat; pay close attention to this: if he had said simply, 'having been outraged, men of the jury, and having suffered many terrible things at the hands of Conon', the thought would have been complete and would have needed nothing further, and he would have had to move on; but suspending it with the consequential clause, in saying 'and having suffered such things', made it follow to add of what sort: 'so that for a very long time neither my family nor any of the doctors expected me to survive.' This, then, is what the consequential clause can do: to make many words out of one and to produce amplitude. And again in the speech Against Conon, going on, he says: 'and at first they abused me, but in the end they even laid blows on me.' And the simple way would have been to say: 'and they made a great shouting and uproar around the tent'; but the thought would have been complete and like something tossed aside; as it is, the consequential clause produced the amplitude: 'and they made such shouting and uproar around the tent'; for upon the suspension by the consequential clause another thought must by all means be brought in: '[they made such shouting] that both the general and the taxiarchs came.' And another consequential clause in the speech: the simple way would have been to say 'they treated me badly, jumping on me and beating me'; but the amplitude from the consequential clause: 'they treated me so, jumping on me and beating me, that they split my lip.'

Enumeration is also a figure of amplitude. An example of this is in the speech On the False Embassy, where he says: 'for what, then, must one take account from an ambassador?' And the simple way would have been to say thus: 'for what he reported, for what he persuaded [you of]'; but the amplitude lies in the enumeration: 'first, then, for what he reported; second, for what he persuaded [you of]; third, for what you instructed him.' And again elsewhere: 'for what reason, then, did I go through these things? First, so that you may know and learn; second, for a reason no less than this.'

Omissions also produce amplitude, as in the speech Against Meidias: 'all the annoyance he caused, either by opposing the discharge of my chorus members from military service, or by putting himself forward for election as overseer for the Dionysia, and all the other such things, I shall pass over'; and again: 'that he contrived an indictment for desertion against me and hired the man who did it, that foul and all too obliging fellow, the dust-cloud Euctemon, I shall pass over.' One must know that some omissions are indefinite, others by species. Indefinite ones are such as: 'I could not tell you all the gifts he received from both sides, nor would you wish to hear it'; it is chiefly the genus that makes [them so]. Such omissions, then, produce amplitude by their indefiniteness; and the omissions by species are such as: 'Olynthus and Apollonia and the thirty-two cities in Thrace I pass over.' And some omissions come at the beginning, like this one, 'Olynthus and Apollonia', others at the end, as where he says: 'his campaigns against the Illyrians and Paeonians and wherever else one might name, I leave aside.' Among those at the end is also this omission, which has amplitude: 'though I have many other things to show which these men have done, and in which they have lied, I would gladly tell you of them; but since you consider them outside the matter, I shall pass them over.' You will increase amplitude if you do not state the omissions bare, but also add the reasons for them, as in the speech Against Leptines: 'how he drew you up against all the Peloponnesians at Thebes, and how he killed Gorgopas on Aegina, and all that he did in Cyprus, and after that in Egypt, and that, having gone through almost every land, nowhere did he disgrace the city's name or himself' — and the reason why he omits [these]: that it is impossible to speak of them as they deserve — 'and it would be a great shame if, when I spoke of these things, they should appear less than the opinion each of you holds of him.'

Divisions also produce amplitude most of all, when you do not bring in the thoughts one at a time, but divide them and set them against each other, as in the Philippics: 'but if he has resolved that he must always be doing something greater than what he has, while you [have resolved] that none of our affairs should be taken in hand.' This, then, is dividing the thought between persons; and another, divided between person and place: 'so, since you are unable to sail out from here, while there is no help ready there.' Isocrates greatly enjoys producing amplitude by this manner of divisions; for the sake of example, one or two from Isocrates' On the Peace: 'for we have come to this'; and the division: 'through neglect of our own affairs, and desire for those of others'; then, telling the absurd things that resulted for them from these, he divides: 'they filled the public tombs with citizens, and the phratries and the deme registers with foreigners.' Then again, enumerating what befell the Lacedaemonians from their rule of the sea, he says: 'the sea filled them, the private citizens with injustice, lawlessness, idleness, love of money'; and he did not simply set 'the community of the city' against this and this, but subdivided it again: 'and the community of the city with contempt for some, and desire for the possessions of others.' But subdivisions too can produce amplitude, for example: 'not only did you do this, but also this'; 'that we are seen giving up not only cities and places of which we were once masters, but also the allies and opportunities provided by fortune.' And in the speech Against Leptines: 'you must consider not only that Leucon should not be wronged, but also whether anyone else [should be]'; and this is what is introduced concerning Epicerdes. And again: 'it is right, men of Athens, to beware of wronging not only those who privately resolved to benefit you and made themselves useful, but also the many who furnished whole cities, their own homelands, as allies to us in the war against the Lacedaemonians'; and again: 'Conon, then, was honoured at that time not only by us for doing what I have related, but also by many others.'

Bringing in the thoughts by juxtaposition also has amplitude, when one does not simply say 'this happened and this', but 'instead of this happening, this happened, and instead of this, this', as Demosthenes in the speech On the False Embassy: 'for instead of seeing Thespiae and Plataea resettled, you heard that Orchomenus and Coronea had been enslaved.' Isocrates too enjoys producing amplitude by the figure of juxtaposition: 'for instead of garrisoning the citadels of others, they saw the enemy become masters of their own; and instead of taking children as hostages', he says, 'they saw their own reared unworthily; and instead of farming the lands of others, for many years it was not even possible for them to see their own.'

Completions also produce amplitude, in the speech Against Conon: 'that, then, it was not after receiving moderate and slight blows' — and the opposite of 'not after receiving slight blows': 'but after coming back [near death]' — and he adds what led him to act: 'on account of the outrage and wantonness of these men, I have brought a suit far smaller than is fitting'; now the summing-up, agreed upon for intensification: 'I think it has become clear to you from many points.' Since you now follow, I have shown you the individual observations on amplitude in the parts in which the completion occurs; for to state the completion itself would have been like this: 'that, then, it was not after receiving moderate and slight blows, but after coming back [near death], on account of the outrage and wantonness of these men, that I have brought a suit far smaller than is fitting, I think has become clear to you.' There are also other completions that produce wonderful amplitude, at once completing and rounding off what has been said and providing a transition to what is next brought in, as in the speech On the Crown: 'the things, then, that I furnished to justify writing such things about me are, among many others, these and things like these'; up to this point is the completion; then the announcement of what follows: 'but what you all know, this I shall now tell.'

And putting thoughts in oblique construction belongs above all to amplitude, so that even in narratives, if the thoughts are put obliquely, it produces wonderful amplitude, as Demosthenes in the speech Against Aeschines: 'and having Ischander, son of Neoptolemus, as his second actor'; he did not put it directly, saying 'he approached the council', but again put it obliquely: 'and approaching the council, and approaching the people about these matters.' And another in oblique construction: 'and having persuaded you to send ambassadors everywhere about these matters'; and another of the same kind: 'and reporting'; and another after these: 'and relating how greatly those who take bribes and receive money from Philip wrong the whole of Greece, not their own homelands alone.' And how does Aeschines [do it]? 'For Amyntas having recently died'; and another oblique construction: 'and Alexander, the eldest of the brothers'; 'and Perdiccas and Philip being children.' And another oblique construction: 'and Pausanias coming down to seize their rule, being an exile, but strong because of the moment'; and again oblique construction upon oblique construction: 'and many working with him, and having a Greek force, and having taken Anthemus and Therma, and the Macedonians not being of one mind, but most of them favouring the side of Pausanias; at this juncture'; and he put it directly and gave us rest: 'the Athenians elected Iphicrates general.'

In expression, amplitude arises in this way, when one uses equivalent terms. One must know that of equivalent terms some are set side by side according to what is consequent, others according to the opposite of what is consequent. According to what is consequent, where he says 'you are strong and trust yourself', and again 'the wantonness and the outrage', and again 'the wealth and the abundance', or 'the companions and friends'. And equivalents according to the opposite of what is consequent, again: 'seeing these things neglected and receiving no help.' And this too is an equivalent: 'all of you and the whole people.'

One must also know that this observation is inferior to none: that solemnity and amplitude share in everything; for in whatever things they are composed of, they share with one another, and one must think about them in this way.
On credibility.

Credibility arises in two ways, by thought and by figure. By thought in this way, when one commends one's own just case in advance, as being true and easy to show, as in the speech Against Aristocrates: 'I take my speech to be very short, men of Athens, and easy, concerning the decree having been proposed contrary to this law.'

It is also credible to pretend that the points in question are more evident than those already proved and agreed, as in the speech Against Aristocrates: having proved the illegality, while the inexpediency remained to be examined, he credibly took it up and pretended that the inexpediency was even more evident than the illegality, the point in question [more evident] than the one proved, where he says: 'for though the decree is so strongly contrary to the laws, it is more inexpedient than illegal.'

It also belongs to credibility to use oaths and curses, for example: 'I call upon all the gods and goddesses who hold the land of Attica, in your presence, and Apollo the Pythian, who is ancestral to the city, and I pray to all of these, if I should speak the truth to you, and spoke it then at once before the people, to give me good fortune and safety; but if out of enmity or for the sake of private rivalry, to make me without profit of all good things.' And again: 'First, men of Athens, I pray to all the gods and goddesses that as much goodwill as I continually hold towards the city and all of you, so much may be granted me from you for this contest.' And in the speech Against Conon: 'and if I swear truly, may many good things come to me and may I never again suffer any such thing; but if I swear falsely, may I perish utterly, myself and whatever I have or am going to have.'

It also belongs to credibility when one takes in the judgements of those hearing these things on what one says, as though the matters were agreed among them too, as when he says in the speech Against Aristogeiton: 'that this matter has long been judged, in each man's nature, at home.' And again: 'you jurors have come knowing better than us accusers that this man is a debtor to the treasury, and is registered on the Acropolis, and is not permitted to speak, so that each of you holds the place of an accuser and knows the just case, and has no need to learn it.' And: 'and if you know me to be such a man; for I have not lived anywhere else.'

It also belongs to credibility to speak with confident assurance about the facts, as when you say: 'Know well, then, men of Athens, that you have been deceived, and hear from me the reasons why you have naturally suffered this.' And in the speech On the False Embassy he at once spoke with assurance: 'that I shall prove this man to have done many terrible things and to deserve the utmost punishment, I am confident and fully trust.' And in the speech Against Stephanus: 'I shall show you that this Stephanus here has given false testimony, and has done this out of greed for base gain, and is becoming his own accuser; so great is the plainness of the matter.'

It is also credible when one strongly denounces as terrible and grievous the things from which one wishes to seem furthest removed, for example: 'for he charged me with things that a man of sound mind would shrink even from saying, that I had killed my own father.' And in the speech Against Midias: 'for the wretched and unfortunate man, on whom a terrible and grievous charge had fallen.' And again: 'he let neither the gods nor piety stand in the way of such a speech, nor did he hesitate, nor was he ashamed before the very people to whom he was speaking.'

It is also credible to anticipate by assessing a penalty and fixing punishments against oneself on the matters one recounts, for example: 'I sailing as a volunteer, ready to suffer anything whatever.' And again elsewhere, in the Philippics: 'neither now nor hereafter pay attention to me as to a man of sound mind.'

It is also credibility to assign to oneself more than the truth against one's case, for example: 'there are foreigners who are exempt; I will put them at ten, and, by the gods, as I said just now, I do not think there are five. But of the citizens there are not five or six. So of both, sixteen. Let us make them twenty, or, if you like, thirty.'

It also belongs to credibility to show that the matters one undertakes are difficult, but that one speaks of them because it profits the city that they be spoken, even if one runs some risk oneself, having chosen, for the common advantage, to suffer something too if need be. An example of this is in the deliberative speeches: 'I see how difficult it is to say what is best; for since you have been deceived, and some have chosen this course and others that, if anyone undertakes to say the opposite and you do not wait to learn, he will please neither side and will be slandered before both. Nevertheless I shall choose rather, if this is what I suffer, to seem to talk nonsense, than to allow certain people to deceive you contrary to what I think best.'

It is also credible to anticipate and say yourself whatever another would say in opposing you, as in the speech On the Symmories: what he is managing is that one must oppose those who advise making war on the King; but since there fell against him from the other side the objection 'Are we then not to make war on the common enemy and barbarian?', for this reason he credibly anticipates what someone would have said from that side against the King, and says it himself: 'I consider the King the common enemy of all the Greeks.' Then what he himself now proposes: 'yet I would not on that account urge the others to take up war against him.'

It also belongs to credibility to establish from hearsay whatever you cannot support from elsewhere: 'I for my part heard from some people that they would no longer even grant him the harbours and the markets to draw profit from.' And again: 'as I heard from one of those who had been in the country itself, a man in no way able to lie.' More credible still is to be able to refer it to the hearers themselves, for example: 'having heard it from you, I am able to teach you.' And again: 'things which I myself have heard from you, the older men.'

It also belongs to credibility to add a falsehood on top, as in the speech On the Crown, where he says that Aeschines became an Athenian late: 'late indeed, late, I say', then credibly added a falsehood on top: 'or rather yesterday and the day before, an Athenian and an orator.' And again in the speech Against Aeschines, the true part, 'one of those who came to the audits he has done away with', and what follows he added falsely on top, namely: 'others he goes about threatening.'

It also belongs to credibility to say something as though one had just remembered it, for example: 'I nearly passed over what I most needed to tell you.' Of the same kind is to say something as though searching for it: 'Take also the decree voted for Chabrias. Look and search; it must be here somewhere.' For to bring something in not as prepared but as searching for it on the spot is like improvisation and makes the speech credible.

Above all, it belongs to credibility both to mark out in advance what is being introduced and to use hyperbole. Marking out, when you say: 'What, then, I think you most of all must guard against, men of Athens, this I still wish to say.' That is, with the preceding words leading into what is about to be introduced. The hyperbole is in what follows, for example: 'for if one should grant that all that Leptines will say about the law, teaching you that it is well enacted, is true, one shameful thing at least could not be removed, whatever happened, which will befall the city through the law becoming valid.'

It is also credible to concede and assent to some of the objections that our opponents seem to make against us, as in the speech Against Midias: the objection from the other side, 'perhaps he will now say such things as that everything I say is premeditated'; then his own concession with hyperbole: 'but I admit that I have premeditated and rehearsed as much as was possible for me.'

Credibility arises by figure in this way, when one uses for matters in question the figures suited to matters agreed, as there: 'Do you not see and reckon the coming season of the year, by which some think they must leave the Hellespont bare of you?' And again, for the sake of credibility, he introduces by the figure as agreed: 'for you know this, I suppose, that for each of those who wrong you there is one penalty.' And again: 'you know perhaps even without my speech that Chabrias was an excellent man.'

It is also credible by figure when one uses announcement in the speech; for it is very credible to make pledges about the points in question, as in the speech Against Leptines: the point in question is whether they will enact the law being brought in, and he pledges, saying: 'we guarantee, I, Phormio, and anyone else he wishes, that he will enact the law.' And again: 'we guarantee, we promise; let the thesmothetae write this down; let the matter proceed on these terms.'

It also belongs to credibility when one uses concurrence, as in the Philippics, for example: 'but if these things seem to anyone to involve great expense and much trouble' — here the concurrence is 'and he thinks quite rightly.' For he concedes at first what seems to tell against him, so that he may introduce what tells in his favour.

This too is very credible, when one uses omission. The figure belongs also to amplitude, yet, fitting many [qualities] according to different uses, it often has a certain peculiarity in credibility. For when you seem to omit something and do not omit it, there lies the credibility, as in the speech Against Leptines: 'the other things, then, in which this man made himself useful, both he and his ancestors', then he used omission: 'I shall omit.' And again: 'shameful, men of Athens, and bad is the law, like some envy and rivalry', then, having nothing more to say, he credibly used omission: 'and the rest I let pass.'
And for someone to speak against himself in the same way as against his opponents creates credibility in the speech.
On vehemence.

Vehemence arises in three ways: by thought, by figure, by diction. By thought, thus: when one rebukes esteemed persons, for example: 'you have abandoned, men of Athens, the post in which your ancestors left you.' And another again like this: 'for you alone of the Greeks are idle', and again: 'and of this too you are the cause, having first allowed them to strengthen their city after the Persian Wars.' You also create vehemence when you do not hesitate to disparage esteemed things or persons; for example, praising the ancestors is a most esteemed thing, yet how did Demosthenes disparage it right at the beginning? 'Those who praise the ancestors seem to me to give a gratifying speech, but not to do what is advantageous for those whom they eulogise.' And in general rebuke has vehemence, as in that passage: 'both seem to me to err, those who have spoken for the Arcadians and those who have spoken for the Spartans.'
And to disparage esteemed persons as being in an absurd state creates vehemence, for example: 'but you, the people, enervated, stripped of money and allies, in the role of servant and appendage.'

And when one makes an outlandish comparison, it makes the speech vehement, for example: 'like a scorpion with its sting raised, darting this way and that, watching for whom he may bring into misfortune by rubbing some harm on him.' And again: 'for neither is a knife that does not cut any use to a cook, nor is a sycophant who will sell these things of any use to one who wishes evils and troubles to come upon everyone through him.' And again elsewhere: 'but we are like men who have drunk mandrake or some other such drug.'

There is vehemence also when one expresses excessive indignation, for example: 'for this admits of no excess of foulness', and again elsewhere: 'for this indeed is the extreme', and again: 'it falls short in nothing of the extreme of outrage.'

And in general, wherever the accusations are made over wrongs that are more or less agreed upon, because the wrongs are manifest, the speech attains vehemence, as both in the speech Against Meidias and in that Against Aristogeiton. But the most important thing to know is this: when the points at issue are not strong on either side, and it is open to the other side [to argue] that they are not manifest, yet the speaker frames his speech as though the points at issue were more or less agreed, such is the speech Against Meidias.

Vehemence arises by figure thus: when one uses exclamatory figures, for example: 'shameful, men of Athens, and bad is the law, and like a kind of envy and contentiousness.' And again: 'keep him away, then, keep him away from the speeches on behalf of the peace.' And in the speech Against Meidias: 'and I, suffering these things and being harried in the way that I am now relating to you.' And in the speech On the False Embassy: 'nothing more terrible than these things has happened, men of Athens.'

The figure of apostrophe also has vehemence: 'you, most abominable of all men, though free speech has been shut off for you not by lattice-gates or doors, which one might even push open, but by so many and such great debts, and these lodged with the goddess, you force your way inside these bounds and approach the very things from which the laws drive you away, roped off as you are from all rights in the city.' And again in the speech Against Meidias: 'what are you saying, you abominable creature? Will you ask [them] to pity your own children, or [ask] these men to pity you, men whom you have publicly abused?'

By expression, that is, by diction, vehemence arises when you use hyperboles in the speech, for example: 'rich, bold, proud, loud-mouthed, violent, shameless.' And this too has hyperbole, when you say: 'the city does not contain him.' 'Neither Greece nor the barbarian land contains the man's greed.' And where he says: 'to do obeisance to those who commit outrage, as among the barbarians, and not to defend oneself, will be best.'

All things that heighten produce vehemence in the speech, as in the speech Against Conon: 'I was dragged and stripped, and having gone out healthy I came home carried', and where he speaks about his mother; for he did not say 'had gone out', but, more emphatically in the choice of word, 'my mother had rushed out'; for the emphasis lies in the word.

And just as we have often said that tropes have great power in many places, so too in vehemence, when, for the sake of vehemence, he speaks against the wickedness of Aristogeiton: 'a huckster and a dealer, all but holding scales and weights, he sold everything.'
On emphasis.

In a certain way the three virtues of speech, vehemence, emphasis and asperity, even if they differ in name, at any rate in their force share very closely with one another in very many respects: vehemence is emphatic speech, and asperity has the force of vehemence. Nevertheless, you will create emphasis by thought when you state facts that are continuous and follow one upon another, as in the speech Against Leptines: 'he defeated the Spartans, then, in a sea battle, and took forty-nine triremes captive, and he captured most of the islands, and brought three thousand captives here, and produced a hundred and ten talents from the enemy'; and again: 'seventeen cities he captured, seventy triremes he took, a hundred and ten talents he produced, so many trophies he set up.' Each of these is a fact in itself, but the fact that one is brought on continuously after another has created the emphasis.

Marking [things] by their qualities also creates emphasis, where he says: 'a terrible sight', and again: 'a terrible and grievous disease, needing much vigilance and correction from you.' And in the speech Against Meidias: 'but what seems to me terrible, men of Athens, and outrageous, is that an impiety, not merely a wrong, has been committed by this man.'

By figure emphasis arises when one uses demonstratives, for example: 'this law, men of Athens, is both old and good.' And again in deliberative speeches: 'you see this city, in this [city], being of such great size.' 'Do you see Aristolochus the son of Charidemus? Once he had a field, but now many [own it]; that man, being in debt to many, acquired it.'

Questions too will create emphasis for you, as in the speech Against Boeotus on the name: 'but if someone were to ask you, Boeotus, how you have now come to be of the tribe Acamantis, of the deme Thoricus, and the son of Mantitheus, would you have anything else to say except that Mantitheus adopted me also in his lifetime?' And in the speech On the Crown: 'if you do not believe it, ask them; or rather, I will do this for you', and then the question: 'does Aeschines seem to you, men of Athens, to be a hireling or a guest-friend of Alexander?'
And when one uses continuous refutations, emphasis arises in the speech.
By expression emphasis arises in the same way as asperity and vehemence do.
On forcefulness.

Forcefulness arises by thought alone; if anyone thinks it arises by anything else, he is badly mistaken. Forcefulness is when one prepares in advance, from far off, something useful to oneself, as in the speech Against Aristocrates, where Demosthenes, wishing to show that it is dangerous and against the city's interest for one of the Thracian kings to become sovereign, takes it from far off and establishes that the weakness of Cersobleptes, whose general is Charidemus, is the safeguard of the Chersonese, so that the opposite, namely that most of the kings be overthrown and [the power] pass to one man, Cersobleptes, through Charidemus, is a danger to the Chersonese. So from far off he prepared in advance [the argument] that to vote that whoever kills Charidemus be liable to seizure makes Cersobleptes formidable, and that he, once grown strong, will overthrow the other kings, through whom the Chersonese is kept safe. 'So that it may become clear to you also from the very things that have been said, it is necessary first of all to state and show what it is that has made you hold the Chersonese securely; for by learning this you will also see the wrong clearly. This, then, men of Athens, is it: that on the death of Cotys, Berisades, Amadocus and Cersobleptes became three kings of Thrace instead of one; for it has come about that they are rivals to one another, while they court and cultivate you. Certain people, then, wishing to stop this and to overthrow the other kings and hand over the whole rule to Cersobleptes, are contriving to have this preliminary decree passed for themselves.'

Forcefulness is also to refute from far off, before stating it, something that tells against oneself. 'How, then, when you had perceived from my speaking in support of Philocrates that I had taken bribes, did you, having been elected to our embassy, consent to serve as envoy with us, and not swear yourself off?' Setting this objection against himself without having stated it as a proposition, he then brought on the solution: 'for I had agreed with the captives that I would bring ransom, and for this reason I went on the second embassy, so that I might ransom them and save them as far as I could; it would therefore have been terrible to break my word and abandon fellow citizens in misfortune.' It would have seemed to be a proposition, and [he would have seemed] to be inventing it to fit the occasion after changing his position; but as it is, before stating the proposition, he set out in anticipation the matter of the captives by a comparison of the time periods: 'during the time we spent in Macedonia, what did each of us choose to do? I, then, [chose] to rescue the captives, to seek them out, and to spend money of my own, while this man, you will hear presently what he kept doing.' Having prepared in advance the matter of the captives in this way, he now brings forward the proposition itself, with the solution already prepared: 'and when this man presently says to you, "Why ever, Demosthenes, if, as you say, you knew from my speaking in support of Philocrates that we were doing nothing sound, did you go again with us on the embassy after this, the one for the oaths, and not swear yourself off?", remember this: that I had agreed with those whom I myself ransomed that I would come and bring ransom and save them as far as I could; it would therefore have been terrible to break my word and abandon fellow citizens in misfortune.'
On carefulness.

Carefulness arises, in general, in three ways: by thought, by figure, by expression. By thought, when one does not separate the ideas from one another or set them apart, but joins them to one another; and when one uses mixed and varied conceptions, as if bringing [them] in from outside and taking them up from what remains; and when one does not set out the facts bare, but together with what accompanies them and with the nature of the facts, for example stating either the manner, or the time, or the cause, or the place; and when one uses tropes, carefulness arises.
By figure, carefulness arises in this way: by using divisions.
By expression, carefulness arises when the expression is dense and closely packed, and when it is verbal rather than nominal.
On sweetness.
Sweetness arises, in general, in three ways: by thought, by figure, by expression. By thought, in this way: when one uses conceptions from outside, for example from histories, proverbs and myths.
By figure, sweetness arises when one uses novel expressions.
By expression, when one uses tropes, but tropes that are not harsh but subdued, and when one uses diction that is stirred.
On clarity and purity.

Clarity and purity arise by thought, by figure and by expression. By thought, in this way: when one does not invert the facts, but goes through them in the order in which they were done; and when one does not insert ideas from outside into them, but goes through the very things that were done; and when one goes through what is known as known and what is disputed as disputed.
By figure, clarity and purity arise in this way: when one uses recapitulations, and when, passing from one matter to another, one uses a completion for the one and an announcement for the other.

By expression, in this way: when one uses more common words, and those that are strongly significant and show the facts more vividly; and when one uses narrative figures; and when one uses equivalent terms as little as possible [he means tropical and metaphorical expressions equivalent, that is, to the proper ones]; and when one uses milder [words] instead of harsh ones.
On brevity and conciseness.

Brevity and conciseness arise by thought and by diction. By thought, in this way: when one engages at once with the necessary parts of the facts, and when one does not use everything as principal, but some things as principal and others not so.

By diction, brevity and conciseness arise when one uses not periphrastic expressions but direct ones; when one does not contend with the diction by setting equivalent terms side by side, but, having made the matter clear with the word that signifies it, is done with it at once and in few words; and when one does not strive for ambition in diction, but also looks to the facts.
On the restraint of speech.

Speech is restrained, in general, in three ways: by thought, by figure, by diction. By thought, in this way: when one does not give way to conceptions from outside; and when, compelled to use some conception, one does not simply bring it in, but indicates that one was compelled, and softens it; and when one does not simply set down ideas cut off from the subject matter, but as close to it as possible.
By figure, restraint arises in this way: when one breaks up the consequential clauses of the sentences, when one uses apologies, when one uses corrections.

By expression, in this way: when one uses the proper word for the facts instead of the trope, and when one uses hyperboles less; and when one is at some point compelled to use some tropical hyperbole, one apologises. The way in which this is done is easy to show.

There are also other forms concerning speeches, and likewise concerning poetry, both far from and near to one another, which it is not easy to grasp all at once; but each man, cutting off a part, won renown for that, though I except the poet Homer from this account. So when someone makes it his ambition to go through all these fine qualities and to blend every mixture in speeches, he must first render characters suited to the occasions, and then the pairings: where there is precision, adding charm there; where brevity, speed there; to elaboration, clarity; grace where there is solemnity; where invention, handling there; where there are bold strokes, safety there. Here every listener grows dizzy and does not know what to make of it, but, like men encircled in a battle line, they are thrown into confusion, and each praises according to his nature: one the precision of the diction, another the subtlety of the thought, another [the parts] as charming, and another something else.
