And since the parts of virtue are also found in the form of rhetoric, the orator too would be of this kind: for it belongs, I think, to the prudent and temperate man to recognise the worth of each matter, to the just man to render what is fitting both to himself and to others, and to the brave man not to fear to speak the truth; and the same man is indignant at all that is opposite to these. Fittingly he is bound by certain [restraints], so that it may not seem that the speeches are foreign to the speaker and draw after them a reputation greater than the truth. These things too, then, belong to the orator: to see what is best, to speak it out and handle each matter, to keep the harmonies and the arrangement and choice always fitting to the occasion, to chasten, to exhort, to restrain, to bring in whatever is needed; and to show speeches that wholly share in beauty, intelligence, strength and temperance, by the density of the enthymemes, the proportion of the words, the harmonies, the ingenuity, the figures, the graces of the headings, of the intention, and of the themes.

For some [themes] are encomiastic, some deliberative, some judicial. Of the judicial, some concern substance, some particularity, some quality; and again of judicial speeches some, I think, are very short, some very long, and some in between these. Deliberative speeches are by nature shorter than the judicial, although there are also deliberative speeches somewhat longer than judicial ones, and judicial ones [longer] than those of the same kind, and some close in length; but neither are the latter set apart from the former, nor do the former differ at all from the latter: for by the chance of the matters they run both to less and to more, each beyond itself and beyond the other, while by its whole nature the one is somewhat longer than the other. And this is a sign: since the deliberative speech is not much shorter than the longest contentious one, so [the art] wishes the contests to be distinguished from one another not only by their forms but also by their proportion, broadly speaking. The adviser, then, will say all that he must, but will say it in fewer words than one contesting a lawsuit; while the litigant will say everything just as the adviser does.

Since, then, there are three kinds of speech and of the fortune of the matters concerning them, I say that other kinds fall into the same [speech], which one must take up and blend; just as Demosthenes' speech about the guard granted to Charidemus shares somehow in the three genres: for the part on illegality is in itself plainly judicial, proving that Aristocrates proposed contrary to the laws; the part on expediency, again, has a certain deliberative character, that Cersobleptes must not be allowed to grow greater; and third, in addition to these, there is what belongs to the encomiastic manner, the censure of Charidemus. All these are brought round into the one judicial [form], and there has come about such a blending and mixture of them, and neither is one like the other, but it differs as much as the matter requires, and the kinds are in no way broken off from one another, so that the whole speech would not be consistent with itself.

One must know that the themes of deliberative questions are these: the just, the expedient, the possible, the easy, the necessary, the safe, the honourable, the pious, the holy, the pleasant, and their opposites. The just is constituted by law, nature and custom; the just by law is seen in command and prohibition. The expedient is constituted from four topics, which are these: keeping the goods we have, acquiring the goods we do not have, escaping the evils that surround us, preventing the evils that are coming upon us. The possible is constituted from persons and what is brought to bear on them. The easy is constituted from these: from needing fewer labours or less expense or fewer dangers or anything else of the kind, as against the opposite. The necessary is constituted from someone's being unable, to all appearance, to do what he wishes otherwise than as necessity compels; from being unable to escape fears, disturbances, griefs and the violence in necessities in any other way than this, or as necessity compels; from defining the thing as altogether necessary, for example dying. The safe is constituted from these: there being no fear of suffering anything from gods, or enemies, or any who are stronger, or the law. The honourable is constituted, to put it in a definition, from the praises of good things. These are piety, honours, praises, memorials, friendships, pledges, the glories of ancestors, and the achievements already present in deeds, which one must not disgrace, and keeping what is fitting in life, such as good order, simplicity, truth, friendship; and it would be so if, besides these, the honourable is constituted also from praising and comparing the deeds of others. And in general whatever accords with virtue and is the work of virtue: for all these belong to the honourable. Opposed to these are their opposites. The pious is constituted from the natural observance of what is just and lawful towards the gods. The holy is constituted from the keeping of what is just towards the fatherland and its welfare, and towards parents, benefactors, teachers, and those beneath the earth. The pleasant is constituted from the enjoyment of pleasures; of pleasures some arise from taste, some from sight, some from hearing, some from the mind, and these happen to be greater and purer.

Of the encomiastic [kind], since it lies outside disputed questions, the themes are drawn either from persons or from matters; from these come praises, encomia and hymns, and what is opposed to them, censures. Of the laudatory [forms], then, one is called praise, another hymn, another encomium: a hymn is addressed to the gods and has nothing opposed to it; praise is what is given for small things, such as 'well' and 'finely', for these too are laudatory, and again 'he is good', 'he is brave', 'he is just'; the encomium raises [its subject] to something greater, and therefore encomia proceed by detailed narration. Praises are handled in four ways: by amplification, by omission, by comparison, by euphemism. By amplification, for instance, if someone praising the works of the ant should wish to say that it is most thrifty in gathering its crops and in storing them away, and more than that, good at foreseeing the seasons the gods send and most prudent in preparing for the right times, and whatever else one might find in amplifying the ant. By omission, when we pass over the awkward things belonging to those we praise, and whatever one might say in censure, and set forth only what deserves praise; for instance, if in praising Alexander we were to recount his other deeds, how he crossed the Granicus, how he advanced as far as Cilicia, how he subdued all the nations as far as Ocean, but were to pass over the killing of Cleitus and his zeal for drinking-bouts, and that he changed into Median dress and claimed to be prostrated before like the king of the Persians, and all such things as belonged to him. By comparison, when, wishing to show the deeds of the one praised as greater, we demonstrate it from comparison with other things, as Demosthenes, wishing to show the great worth of Conon's works on the building of the walls, says they were better than those of Themistocles. By euphemism, when, not passing over the awkward things, we recount them in a more favourable light; for instance, if in praising Alexander we were to say that the seizure of Helen was not a wrong, nor adultery, nor any offence against Menelaus, who had been his host, but that he desired to become a kinsman of Zeus by marriage; and again of Helen, that she did no wrong in leaving her husband, her daughter and her home, but was eager to become famous.

For praising not offensively, yet being able to do so in as many ways as need arises in political questions, there are these methods. First, when someone appears to have been brought to it not as though he had himself planned and prepared it, but as one compelled; second, when someone rejects some things and recounts others; the third method, when before saying anything he asks pardon of the judges for what he is about to say; fourth, when he places the praise among things held in common; fifth, when he declares that it befits the hearers themselves too to welcome these things; sixth, when one is able to show that his opponents also do the same thing, and declares it outrageous that they do it for their own advantage, but he may not.

On censure. Censure is handled in three ways: for one can censure by amplification, by omission and by comparison, but no longer by euphemism, but rather by the opposite of euphemism, dysphemism. Censure by dysphemism occurs when things that were done well are reported in a less favourable light; for instance, if someone were to say that Menelaus marched against Troy not for great matters, not out of indignation at the outrages the barbarian had committed against Greece, but for the sake of one woman, and she not a good one, as the tragic poet too says: 'O you who led an army for a woman's sake, and nothing else.'
On composition and phrasing.

Composition is, first, continuous, strung along through many [clauses] in succession, as in 'For a grievous sickness, men of Athens, has fallen upon Greece'; second, loose, at times diffuse, as in 'Let it be, let these things happen, I do not object'; and third, periodic, which is an arrangement of cola and commata, a phrasing rounded off to complete a thought, as in 'Believing these matters, men of Athens, both serious and necessary for the city, I shall try to say about them what I think expedient.'

A colon is a composition of two or more words, as in 'I do not lack a pretext for helping Nicias.' A comma is a part of a colon, set either on its own, as in 'Know yourself' and 'Nothing in excess', or with others, as in 'I entreat you by your children, by your wives, by the good things you have.'

A period may consist of one colon, as in 'For to prosper beyond one's desert becomes for fools an occasion of thinking ill'; some of two cola, as in 'For not to give something from the beginning is the act of men who have used judgement, but to take it from those who hold it is the act of the envious.' Of three: 'Judges, chiefly because I think it expedient that the law be repealed, and then also for the sake of Chabrias' son, I agreed with these men to speak with them as best I could.' Of more: 'Those who praise your ancestors, men of Athens, seem to me to make a pleasing speech, but not one that benefits those whom they extol.'
Continuous and loose composition would suit narrated actions and emotions; periodic composition suits epideictic speeches, proems and enthymemes.

Phrasing becomes unclear when one uses language that is too archaic and ambiguous, as in 'O Zeus, grant that I bring down the boar' [or 'grant that the boar bring me down']; or in another way, as regards time, cause or place.
Phrasing is redundant if it doubles a word without need, as in 'I spoke, I said, I told'; and if what we said about the foregoing we say again afterwards.
Phrasing is idle when it is in barbarous words, newly coined and counterfeit; hence it also appears ill-timed, untimely assigning the names of some things to others and not expressing the matters.

And indeed, if speech had been invented for any other purpose than persuasion, there might perhaps be some dispute; but since it is evident that the whole habit of the power of speech is directed to this one end, one of two things must surely follow: either the speech is not right and does not appear adequate, or it is at once the best and masters its hearers. Speech is a proof of common humanity and of goodwill towards all, not of bitterness or misanthropy.

It is not one thing alone that prevents us from recalling the expedition from Sicily, but first, that one must not change one's mind and reconsider lightly: for that is outrageous. You will amplify this from the quality of the person: for you it is not even equally shameful as for all others. Why? Because you are trusted to be wiser than the rest. Another amplification, again, from the matter: that you did not deliberate about these matters casually or over a short time; and here you will set beside it the material from history. Against this, the first objection: 'But Sicily is hard to take.' We knew this was said before too, both how great its size and how long its coastline, and yet we sent [the fleet]. And indeed it is not hard to take: for its inhabitants are at strife and at war with one another; what difficulty, then, is there in taking an island divided both in resources and in purpose? 'But we have suffered a setback.' But one must not so lightly lose heart; and this you will confirm from a similar thing that happened among the Syracusans, that they too recovered after failing not once but many times; if they did, so can you. What harm, then, comes to them from changing their minds? First, shame, not only at having deliberated badly, but also at seeming less manly than the Syracusans; then you will make the Syracusans despise you. 'But the Lacedaemonians have broken the treaty.' But even then we did not appear to rely on it. 'But the fortification [in Attica] is something new?' What then? Do you think that if they come home they will overcome the Lacedaemonians? And indeed, if they stay within [the walls], it might perhaps even work against us: for it does not benefit the besieged to bring in a great crowd of men. What benefits will come to them from taking Sicily? 'But Gylippus is gathering an army and assembling Sicily?' Then what befitted you, if you were not afraid of running away, but to send another expedition, which will give our citizens no less eagerness than Gylippus gives the Syracusans? For ours will have not only the advantage of strength, but also the awareness of having often been victorious, while they, who thought to retrieve their former position by numbers and then appeared inferior in resources, will reasonably, I think, become inferior in spirit too. The remaining question is from the outcomes. 'What will be gained, even if we win? For we shall not be able to hold it, being far away.' I would wish your affairs to be in such a state that holding and guarding it is secure. You might say forcefully and in the manner of Demosthenes that nothing else can be done: for we shall seem not to withdraw but to flee, not to have been unable to take it but to have been afraid of suffering; then the Syracusans will not refrain from pursuing us; and if this happens, I fear that the danger will come to us around the Piraeus, and that we shall admit enemy ships into our own harbours, when we ought to be blockading others. These are the points, and in these terms.
Paraphrase.

'Sing, goddess, the wrath of Achilles, son of Peleus.' For it is the task of the Muses to go through in detail the wrath with which Achilles raged at Troy, and what came of it; for those things were neither trivial nor few, but this was indeed the heaviest thing in the war that befell the Achaeans: many of them, and brave men, perished before their time, and many did not even obtain burial, but dogs devoured them where they lay. It was, then, the plan of Zeus, and such great events did not come about by chance, beginning from the time when Achilles son of Peleus and Agamemnon son of Atreus, king of the Greeks, first quarrelled. Which of the gods, then, set them at odds, and from where shall we say the strife began? From Apollo, who, [it is said,] sent a plague upon the Achaeans in anger at their king, and the cause of it was this. An old man named Chryses, a priest of Apollo, came to the camp of the Achaeans to ransom his daughter, a captive, who was with Agamemnon; he held a golden sceptre, and on the sceptre the fillets of the god, and he brought a ransom by no means small, and he supplicated all the Achaeans, but especially the sons of Atreus, praying that they might take Troy and come home safe, and that he himself might be allowed to ransom the girl, and that in any case it was fitting for them to respect the god. At this all the others welcomed his words and shouted their approval that the girl be released to the priest, but Agamemnon would not release her, and threatened him besides, if he should catch him either lingering now or coming back again for the same purpose, that his suppliant's emblem would not protect him, and that his words would no longer be about the girl but about his own safety; and that he would not release her, but would keep her in Argos as his woman, tending his household for life; but if he had any care for his safety, he should go away at once. Hearing this the priest was afraid and at once went away in silence; but when he was some distance from the camp, he now raised every cry, calling on Apollo as Smintheus, Tenedian, Chrysian, Lord of the Fair Bow, naming him by every name: 'If ever, lord, I sacrificed a sacrifice to you or roofed a temple to please you, let this now be granted me in return for those: that the Achaeans wipe away these tears with their own bodies; and may you come against them as an archer.' The god accepts his prayers and at once set out for vengeance.

He had rams, well fed and thick with fleece, wonderful in beauty and size. These I took and quietly bound together in threes; for they were the ones on which the Cyclops slept; the middle one was to carry a man of my companions, and one on either side was a flanker for safety. These, then, served me for the others; I myself made the attempt in this way: there was a ram, huge in every respect and very shaggy; throwing my two hands around its back, I slid down until I too was under its belly; then, turning over, I held on. So that night, suffering thus, we endured.
On simple style.

Since we have shown you the forms of political style and its virtues, you must also hear about the form of simple style; for nothing ought to be examined so much as the qualities of simple and plain style and its differences from political and combative style, which is not easy, because all speech is of one genus and one nature; nevertheless there are certain variations and forms which differ from one another.

All speech evidently consists in thoughts and in expression, which lies in diction, in figure, in rhythm. So it must be said what it is that distinguishes simple speeches from political ones; for the thoughts of simple and of political speeches are not the same. And if the thought is the same, the diction is not the same; or if the diction too is the same, the rhythm is not the same; or if the rhythm too is the same, the figure is not the same.

First, then, one must know, as we may best set it out in summary, that the differences of political style from simple style are taken first from the thoughts. For political thoughts are harsher, more reputable and taken from more reputable sources, and keener, producing their keenness from being rarer and reputable; whereas simple thoughts are plain, common, unremarkable, and these taken from unremarkable arguments. About the thoughts, then, to say a few things out of many, this is it.

The next difference concerns treatment; for just as in political style there is a certain treatment, so also in simple style. The difference in treatments is this: in political style they must be evident; for so the speech would proceed in a political manner, if the hearers follow the questions at issue; but in simple style this is not so: rather the lines of inquiry are sometimes hidden, and one does not even know what the speaker means to say, because the speech seems to follow no design.

The figures in political style are harsh, vehement, refutative, forceful; in simple style relaxed, plain, showing no refutation or scrutiny, but more ordinary and easygoing; for those make the speech intense and political, these make it simple, being as it were private and conversational.

Nor is the diction the same for them, but there is a difference in diction also; for in political style sometimes the thought is completed, and sometimes one must add another thought to it; for the speech must proceed with all security and tension. But in simple style no longer so; rather the diction seems to proceed as it happens, showing a relaxed manner and no studied care in the diction. Further, in political style, whatever one wishes to signify, just that and only that must be shown by the diction; but in simple style a single expression sometimes signifies one, two, or three things. Beauty in diction is produced by the juxtaposition of words, as 'horse-herd of horses', 'swine-herd of swine'.

And concerning rhythms likewise we say there is some difference of political style from simple, and in general the difference of simplicity from political style is that it belongs to simplicity for the speech to move straight on and always draw the ear along evenly, with no breaks in the speech anywhere and no resistance anywhere to the ear; but where, as the speech proceeds, a turn back has occurred and something as it were has resisted the ear from the break at the turn, there the figure is combative and the speech has already become more political in rhythm; for such things always make the hearer turn and do not let him simply follow along, which is what simplicity achieves.

As Xenophon in the Symposium (for I shall now set out examples of these for you, so that the principles of simplicity too may become clearer to you): 'Women, however, especially if they happen to be brides, like the wives of Niceratus here and Critobulus, have no further need of perfume.' And the turn: 'for they themselves smell of it.' This must be understood thus: these women have no need of perfume from a man, for they have it of themselves, being brides. The turn is worth observing: for it belonged to simplicity to go as far as 'have no further need of perfume', but the reason added at the turn, 'for they themselves smell of it', made the speech very brisk, and the speech is in danger of having become political in rhythm.

Again, the thoughts concerning expression belong to simple style, for instance to use, if it so happens, even less reputable thoughts. Thus Xenophon, wishing to establish that Cyrus is worthy of much esteem, consider how he managed this. For the proposition is political, and the proofs most political, that Cyrus became worthy of much esteem; but of the thoughts some were political, others simple. Political are such as these: 'Cyrus became worthy of much esteem; for he accomplished most easily what is most difficult.' And what is most difficult? 'To rule men.' Up to this point the confirmation is political. If you were treating it politically, you would have said thus: 'Cyrus became worthy of much esteem; for what was most difficult, this he accomplished: to rule men. Why? Because men are not readily willing to be ruled, but many dominions and many tyrannies have been overthrown by those unwilling to be ruled.' Up to here the thoughts are political.

But when you come to the confirmation of the difference and say, 'For it is easier to rule cattle and sheep and every herd than a man,' then, I say, you are leading the speech away into simpler thoughts; for they belong to character and manner, which is what preserved the simplicity of the speech. The political speaker, then, having set forth a proposition, adds what confirms it, always selecting the more political of the thoughts; for instance, to speak in terms of the outcomes is not more political, nor would a political speaker say 'herdsmen as rulers', or again, 'we have never yet perceived herds banding together'; but this writer, in keeping with what befits himself, provided the distinctive element in his arguments.

Where the ideas are shared, neither the diction nor the figure is the same; for when he says, 'It once occurred to us', and 'as many as attempted to be tyrants, some of them were overthrown altogether and quickly', he did not say 'paid the penalty'; and again, 'while others, if they remain rulers for any time at all'; for he did not say 'those who took the cities by force and established the strongest dominions for themselves'.

I have shown you, then, that some thoughts are taken from judgement, while others are thoughts of every kind, and of these some are taken from reputable things, others from small and obscure ones. This, then, is how it stands for you: simple writers use thoughts of every kind, and it is not enough for them to use only those taken from the subject matter, but sometimes also such thoughts as someone else would despise and would not even approach, because they are neither taken from the subject matter and happen to be of little repute; but simple writers do not refrain from these.

Such, then, is the matter of the treatment of thoughts; and further, that what is said to confirm the matter in hand is not said as if toward a proposition, but the speech proceeds with it unclear toward what it is said; for instance, without first stating that he wishes to show Cyrus worthy of much esteem, he brings in 'It once occurred to us', and having first taken up all the preliminary confirmations, from which [it follows that] it is difficult to rule men, more difficult than this or that, he then added, 'But Cyrus ruled very many men; Cyrus therefore became worthy of much esteem.' And this is the treatment of simple style, when what is said is not evident as a proposition.

Often, too, the thoughts must not all be strong, as are those of political speeches, but one should set down some in a subdued way, and those that seem lesser, and some, if possible, such as might even appear worthy of laughter; as also in the Symposium, right at the beginning of the speech, he says: 'But to me it seems that of fine and good men not only what is done in earnest is worth remembering, but also what is done in play.' The thought has to do with character: that one must welcome even what fine and good men do in play. And this is the principle of simple style: not to pursue by every means what is reputable and great, but also what seems trivial and easily despised.

In the delivery, then, neither of the two thoughts is spoken harshly, neither 'It once occurred to us' nor 'But to me it seems'; for since what was said in the Symposium seemed of little repute, to narrate things done in play, and no political speaker would have done this, since it is of little repute, he led in with an apology: 'But to me it seems'. If his speech had begun with a declarative word, such as 'It seems to me', the speech would have become harsher and would have seemed rather to be Critias' than anyone of that sort.

As for figure, [he used] a relaxed figure; for he would not have done it with strain, as one of the political speakers would have said: 'I do not find myself thinking the same as the many about serious men; for the many think nothing else of theirs worth remembering than what is done in earnest, but with me it is not the same way; rather, what is done in play seems to me no less worthy of remembrance than what they might do in earnest.' He did not lead in thus, then, but with a relaxed figure and in a varied way: 'But to me it seems'; then, in keeping with the peculiar character of the speech, words having to do with character, 'of fine and good men'. And again he says, 'When the horse race had ended.' The figure seems relaxed and laid back; a political speaker would not have done it thus, but more tautly, 'when, then, the horse race ended', or in some such way.

The ancients, both simple and political writers, use figures in varied ways; for what makes a speech pungent in political style produces simplicity here. And the rhythm of the delivery must be such as to advance and step forward rather than press on, crowding upon itself; not as in political speeches, where they set down the qualities, when they say 'most terrible of all', or 'at which you will all be indignant', or 'for this is outrageous'; for before stating the fact the political speakers point out its quality, sometimes adding it before the facts, sometimes after the facts. And this too belongs to good rhythm: 'And yet, that he was then, in the mightiest city, judged by the best men, deemed worthy of the finest prize, what further evidence does it need of his excellence before he ruled?' This seems to me to have produced good rhythm in the speech; and what produced the good rhythm is that, having encompassed the thoughts and rounded them off, he brought the thought to a stop, so that what is said after it is no longer joined to it but seems the beginning of another speech; for what does he say? 'And all that [he did] once he was among men.' Xenophon does not use this figure often; for it is harsher and more forensic: we are accustomed to add such things to facts already proved, either as forcing [the point] or as thinking we are saying something very telling. Still, as regards his good rhythm elsewhere, this too is remarkable: that the separate members are continuous in one breath of speech, 'And yet, then; in the mightiest city; judged by the best men; deemed worthy of the finest prize'; and to state many thoughts, each one in a single word, is a mark of power and rhythm.

Simple writers also delight in words, transferring them from one thing to another, as Xenophon in the Agesilaus says, 'He made many lovers of his friendship'; for 'lover' seems to be a word for something else. And again: 'They themselves, catching sight of the followers of the Greeks.' Here again he used a word lesser than the thing; for 'followers' is usually said rather of slaves, but he did not hesitate to call those who follow and the rearmost of the army 'followers'. And in the Memorabilia he says: 'I wonder, then, how ever the Athenians were persuaded that Socrates was not of sound mind concerning the gods.' Here he transferred [the word] as proper to the kind of speech.

One must, however, also observe how, while setting down subdued words for the sake of simplicity, he nonetheless shows in his own manner the greatness of the matter too, as he says at the beginning of the work: 'I have often wondered by what arguments ever those who indicted Socrates persuaded the Athenians that he deserved death from the city; for the indictment against him was something like this: Socrates does wrong, not recognising the gods the city recognises, and bringing in other new divinities; and he does wrong also by corrupting the young.' For 'I have wondered' and 'often' is an emphasis of no small matters, and what was added made it plain. A political speaker would have stated both forces not once but many times; but he was content to state the simple force.

So the ideas are sometimes the same, but the treatment makes the difference in the speech. You see here too the simplicity of the words. For although the subject is worthy of anger and rebuke (for its quality is such: that Socrates, a man of such worth, was condemned), nevertheless, being so simple a man, he says 'I have often wondered', and did not say 'at which one might be angered' or 'at which it is right to rebuke'. For in simple style there is neither force nor passion nor vehemence, nor is the disposition of the matters of such a kind as to mark out in advance the nature of what is brought in; and by this above all the kind of simple style is characterised.

It is fine also to speak of things one knows as though seeking something: 'by what arguments ever'; for he did not say 'by what accusations' or 'by what slanders', which would have suited a political speaker, but 'by what arguments ever they persuaded the Athenians'. And to speak by genus, not by species, 'Anytus and Meletus', but 'those who indicted Socrates'. Alternations too suit simple style: 'does wrong ... does wrong also'.

Then too, of what follows, the proofs are most political; for he seems to show a conflict with the qualities that belonged to [the man]: 'It seems wonderful to me also that some were persuaded that Socrates corrupted the young.' But he does not set down a proposition [first] and then bring in what confirms it; he simply goes through the facts: 'first'. One must observe the treatment of what confirms. A political speaker would have taken the generic points and said how he was temperate, how self-controlled, how he held out against all toils; but he gives the specific points: 'self-controlled in belly and in sexual pleasures', and how he bore winter and summer. Then he mixed the great with the small: 'how then would he have made [them] impious, or lawless, or gluttonous?'

Simple writers often also use ideas brought in from outside, beyond the subject, such as 'we have never perceived herds combining against the herdsman', and all such things. This does not suit a political speaker. For even if political speakers use some ideas from outside, as when one speaks from examples or from histories or from some other such source, still one must use what is attached to the matter; hence they usually treat such things with reasons or announcements, for example, one out of many: 'so that you may know, then, that it does not even accord with the character of the city to make such a law', and then the matters are stated in sequence. In simple style, however, ideas are brought in from almost everything in life. And additions from outside produce grandeur in the speech when the name or place is renowned.

So one must take care throughout that the rhythms, the figures and the words suit simple style, and also the ideas of like rhythm, such as 'things said, things done, things planned'; and as for figures, one should know all those that suit these, but everywhere he preserves the simplicity in them.

We say that in many places the principles are common to simple and political speakers, for instance, to mark out in advance the matters you are going to speak about, to have examined their nature, and [to have examined] the objection to what you say, namely that you are discussing small and trivial things. This too belongs to the simple style: 'Philip the jester came in', and 'he wept', and that 'those reclining at the symposium laughed', and 'the Syracusan put on marvels'. For all these are common to political and simple speakers. But the treatment of what is brought in is peculiar to the man, since the announcement here is also common: 'I wish to make clear the occasions I was present at, from which I know these things.' But what follows the announcement is no longer common but novel; for having made the announcement, he did not state what follows from the announcement, but one of the things concerning him. For what he was present at were the events at Callias' house; but he does not state these at once, but the beginning from which they started to happen; and this kind of thing seems rather to be narration.
On characters.

The simple style too must be varied, especially in this kind, and in places produce solemnity, in places amplitude, in places dignity, in places also display character and charm, and in places laughter too, if possible, as here: 'And Philip the jester, knocking at the door.' For the character is very charming, which belongs to the simple style. For to strip away elaborations, to use the plain words themselves, to follow the nature of the facts and not to fear their smallness and lowliness is the mark of a simple and noble soul; whence also arts of speech were invented, by which even things that do not naturally have grandeur in themselves could acquire grandeur; and sometimes what is shown in them is as it appears, while other things also show something false, as in this: 'You are always mocking us, because you have given Protagoras much silver for wisdom.' For this displays a slight charm, but at the same time has a certain malice.

And some thoughts are such that nothing is understood beneath them, others such that they have character, and the character is not one or simple but varied: one a charming character, another a good character, another displaying sweetness, another kindness, and another is a character of such a kind as to display great solemnity straight away, as in this: 'Autolycus then sat beside his father.' It was very solemn, in the very thought, to make the youth sit beside his father. For such thoughts are solemn, and what above all preserved the character for him was his not using elaboration of his own, as if he had said, 'Autolycus then sat beside his father, as a son ought with his father'; that sort of thing is political. So he left the character and the solemnity to show through.

For some things, as I said, have the character lying beneath and implied, such as the passage mentioned before, 'You are always mocking us'; others are simple and display no malice, as in this: 'some having anointed themselves, others having also bathed'; for this displays nothing more than what happened. But wherever the implications are base and harm the speech, what you bring in must correct the oddity, not simply, but by your own additions, for example: 'Anyone who considered what happened would at once have thought that beauty is by nature something royal', and his own addition: 'especially if one possesses it with modesty and self-restraint, as Autolycus does'; for since the speech is about beauty, one would not refrain from taking such things in a malicious sense.

First, then, the character of the simple style must display kindness; for kindness is excellence of judgement, a choice arising from thought and judgement, and reasonableness of manners. The character must not be signalled by itself at all, but be left to the hearers, so that it may seem free of design. For this reason one must not mark out in advance either terrible things as terrible or frightening things as frightening; it is enough for me only to say, 'Tissaphernes slanders Cyrus to his brother.' For it sufficed him to indicate from the kinship what it is to slander a brother to a brother; but the quality and disposition of it he leaves [the hearer] to consider. If you were presenting it in a combative way, you would have said this: 'what a thing, the most terrible and savage of all, Tissaphernes conceived in his soul'; and if you wished to heighten it and set down the very ideas for which the slander ought not to have happened, you will add: 'respecting neither the gods nor justice, nor [regarding] the deed as most terrible.' For whatever one thinks belongs to character among those who handle political speeches, these things could display character in these writers too, though less so; for among those it is in one manner and shows something else, and among these in another. There one can hint at something, or point to something else, or indicate the very opposite of what you say; but here not, since [it is] a token of simplicity and simplicity of thought. For example's sake, let instances be set down from both. Demosthenes, wishing to display character, what does he say? 'It would be very fitting for you to value such a man most highly, and to call him rightly a benefactor.' But in Xenophon, character, and his hand followed him, so that by examining the arrangement clearly in each of them we would find the character.

Xenophon produces characters first by looking to the peculiarities of the persons about whom he happens to be speaking, then by observing the occasions and besides these the circumstances, what has happened, what is present to them and what accompanies them; reasoning from these he finds how to produce characters in his speeches, and, by Zeus, emotions too. To begin from the books themselves: in the Symposium there is every excellence, and the speech and the simplicity of thought belong to what is said, which one might thus call character; and almost the whole work is conducted in this way. Whence, then, did this come to him? From seeing the occasion and what sort of matter it was and what naturally accompanies it, for instance what sort of thing a symposium is and what tends to be said and done at a symposium. Looking ahead to these he composed the work, as at the very beginning of the work: 'But to me it seems that of gentlemen not only the things done in earnest are worth recording, but also those done in play.' The thought has to do with character, that one should welcome even what great and good men do in play; and the principle of the simple style is that one must not by every means pursue the renowned and the great, but also what seems trivial and contemptible. Again, in the Memorabilia, having understood the peculiarity of Socrates' disposition, he looked to this and conducted the work accordingly; for although the subject is worthy of anger and rebuke, that Socrates, a man of such worth, was condemned, nevertheless he, as a simple man, displayed character here too: he says 'I have often wondered', and did not say 'at which one might be angered' or 'at which it is right to rebuke'. One must, however, also observe how, while setting down subdued words for the sake of simplicity, he nonetheless displayed in the proper place the greatness of the matter; for 'I have wondered' and 'often' is an emphasis of no small matters. Again, in the Education, see how he handled it, saying 'A thought once occurred to us'. The idea is the manner in which Cyrus was reared as a child, what education he shared in, what deeds he did, and how he became the happiest of men; but the man means something else by this. For he has not chosen to praise Cyrus, nor does he care how Cyrus was educated or reared; but since he conducts the work in character, he uses a sketch of what sort of man the good man must be, what rearing and what education he should have, what he must be like while still among children, what when one becomes a youth, and what deeds and pursuits befit the gentleman; and Cyrus is merely a name to him. In the same manner he has handled such discourses in the Memorabilia too; for there he has spoken about many matters, how one should behave towards one's own country and friends and among all one's household; yet it is not said prescriptively, as 'one must behave towards friends in this manner', or 'one must [behave] in this manner towards brothers', or 'there must be no display of statesmanship before a man becomes wise and knowledgeable in affairs'; rather, by supposing other persons he teaches you how such things should be done, as when he speaks of Chaerephon quarrelling with his brother: 'Tell me,' he said, 'are you the only one who does not know that one must behave thus towards brothers?' But he supposed another person. So whenever you wish to conduct a speech in character, you do not introduce it prescriptively, 'one must do this or that', but, supposing another person, you say what you want someone to do: that that man was such and did these things.

The form can seem to supply character in speech not only through simplicity of thought, but also through its opposite, for example by giving someone a harsher and ungentle speech, when some such person is supposed, and again if one were to give fitting words to someone in love, and to all alike with an eye to the emotions, in the way that in the Education [of Cyrus] too he produced emotions from the circumstances, in all that is said about Abradatas and his wife; and the whole excellence lies in preserving and keeping the peculiarities of each, just as they were. So he has made Cyaxares irascible throughout, and another person having some other peculiarity in his soul; for these things produce great characters in speech. And you would preserve [them] if you follow the original thought and the purpose of the speech, considering what it intends for you and looking to the peculiarity of whatever you are speaking about.

Characters in simple writing gain intensity and dignity when someone, displaying his own opinion, leaves the character resting on the thought alone; for example, if you were to say, marking it out: 'The gods gave to Chiron and honoured him, as is right, admiring him for having done the deeds of the honourable justly, because he was just and practised the rest of virtue'; for in these words you display your own opinion of how you are disposed towards such men. But Xenophon was content merely to fall silent on the thought: 'And Chiron, because of his justice', and what follows.

It is characteristic of this man and of all simple writers to supply, as far as possible, a kindly character too, yet not to mark this out by itself. Consider from this the character of simplicity, whether it does not seem to you to belong to a kindly man, when about to die, to wish both his sons to be with him: so kindly and affectionate was Darius that he wished both his sons to be with him. 'When Darius was ill and suspected the end of his life, he wished both his sons to be with him.' This belongs to a kindly character; for he has shown you a fatherly disposition, and the excellence is in the thought, and the character is that of a simple man, as kindly as could be. He also made a kindly character in the Symposium, saying of the woman who was displaying marvellous feats, 'so that the spectators were afraid'. Here too, then, the character appeared kindly, in that the spectators were afraid at the strangeness of the spectacle.

Another character, again, is unseen and hidden, as befits simple speeches: 'So Cyrus goes up, taking Tissaphernes as a friend.' For why must one declare and say 'taking Tissaphernes, the man most plotting against him, as a friend'? Leaving the concealed thing to itself has this character. And pay particular attention to this, that simple men do not mark out their forces, but think fit that they be shown by themselves, unless a suitable occasion appears somewhere, as in the Cynegeticus too: 'I, then, advise the young not to despise hunting.' Here he had occasion, and a marvellous character, after outcomes so great, to speak even prescriptively in his own person: 'I, then, advise.' And when you say the opposite of the emphatic expression and relax the insistence, you produce character; for you do not say 'cling to hunting and be zealous about hunting', but the opposite, 'not to despise hunting or the rest of education'. And this does not let the speech become cheap, when you set something esteemed beside something that does not seem very esteemed: 'not to despise hunting or the rest of education'. To combine the greater with the lesser, and to mix something general with what is said specifically, is the mark of a knowledgeable man: 'for from these men become good in war and in other things'; that is, 'one must do this because of this'. The reason, then, is common to political and simple writers, but the figures differ, in saying it without combining: not 'not only in war but also in other things'.

Again, he made character with sweetness in the Memorabilia, saying, 'and that he would not think he had the greatest gain in acquiring a good friend'; he made a sweet character by naming the thing from the lesser. For instead of saying that all the properties of his friends become his, and the help they give in life, he uses this one expression, which displays both sweetness and character, saying 'acquiring a good friend'.

Also, making reproofs by refutation of the opposite makes character; for example, where it would be natural to say, after [he took care], 'he did not neglect, and he blamed those who neglected', he says 'he did not praise': 'Moreover he himself did not neglect his body, and he did not praise those who neglected it.'

A good and Socratic character is not to lead from the necessary to the necessary, for example: 'He himself discussed human matters, considering what is pious, what impious', then from the neuters to the nouns: 'what is self-restraint, what madness, what courage, what cowardice, what a city, what a statesman.' And in the same passage he also created beauty by cutting off each item.
Ironies too produce characters, for example all the passages where he has made Socrates converse with and instruct the young as if he himself did not know, but rather were searching.

Some words, even apart from the matter, produce character in speech, for example: 'I have met you at a good moment.' Here nothing other than the diction produced character: 'I have met you at a good moment.'

Comparative figures too are very much a feature of simplicity and belong rather to historical prose, but they too supply character, for example: 'rather to these, as if to generals and hipparchs and leaders of zealous pursuits.' But if you had put it the opposite way and said, 'all those who say such men are [good], whom they see rising above the rest in offices and honours and such powers, do not seem to me to act rightly', that manner would have seemed more like Critias than one of the old sophists.

I say, then, that the simple writer also uses unemphatic diction, figure and rhythm, as is the case here too: 'When Darius was ill and suspected the end of his life, he wished both his sons to be with him'; for the rhythm is not such as would be a political orator's, drawn together and gathering the thoughts. Thoughts in the upright case have pungency instead of turning to the oblique; for the oblique would have been 'Darius, being ill'. But simplicity runs the risk of coming very close to cheapness through using most words unemphatically, as here 'was ill' would have been a bare word. For this reason an equivalent term was set beside it, so that it might escape cheapness: 'When Darius was ill and suspected the end of his life.'
On dignity.

Displaying piety towards the gods or kindnesses towards friends has character and dignity too, and one must pay particular attention to such things; for most and the greatest of the precepts are taken in accordance with these ideas. The ideas are taken from what is in the matter itself, and for the ideas too to be expressed as about piety and obedience is very much the preference of simple writers; for, as I said, they do not much enjoy using prescriptive expressions, unless some necessity arises, such as 'one must be pious, obey the gods who rule', but they sketch certain ideas of how one should act, not saying didactically 'one must not do this', but in general: 'to those who do these things, these things usually result'.

Dignity arises in simple speech in many other ways too, but more dignified is when you shift from the person to the things; for it is not the same to say of the person 'the beautiful are kings by nature' (for this is juvenile) as to express it of the thing: 'beauty is by nature something royal'. And for the sake of the dignity in the thought comes the addition after this: 'especially if one possesses it with modesty and self-restraint, as Autolycus does.'

Such combinations also create dignity, for example: 'and a boy, very handsome and playing the cithara and dancing very well'; for combining their different qualities into the same thing removes the difference of kind.

And wherever you introduce things that are going to happen, or are happening, as already having happened, you make the speech dignified, for example: 'When the aulos-girl had played the aulos for them, and the boy had played the cithara.'

And wherever you insert dignified names, you will produce force together with dignity and beauty: 'Zeus and Chiron were brothers, of the same father, but as to mother, the one was of Rhea, the other of a Naiad nymph.' Now making [it] common, 'of the same father', and stating the difference, 'but as to mother, the one of this one, the other of that one', has dignity together with simplicity.

And to say something in general terms is more dignified than in specific terms, for example in general, 'lest he suffer something'; for it is not the same to say in specific terms 'lest he be impaled, lest he be slaughtered'. And [it is dignified] in general to gather all these together and say them in one word, 'lest he suffer something'.
On amplitude.

Amplitude arises also in simple speech, when someone, putting a thought in an oblique case, inserts another, second one, before the sense is completed or the conclusion brought in, so that it seems a single thought, for example: 'The Lacedaemonians deliberating about these things, Agesilaus undertook' (now comes the completing part) 'to cross over', no longer in an oblique case; for it would become long, such as 'having crossed over, to do this and that', but [simply] 'to cross over'.

Every amplitude produces force in speech, but we must consider in what respect the force arising in simple speech differs from that of political speech. Consider, then: 'For faring well beyond one's desert becomes, for the foolish, a starting point for thinking ill.' I say, then, that the assertive form of the figure is not profitable in the simple style; for it confers weight and force, but it is no longer simple or on a human scale, such that one would state the matter so, but elevated and puffed up; nor is the subordinating particle [profitable]: 'for faring well'. For such particles compel the speech, as it encloses the thoughts, to become rounded, hard and tightly bound; hence one should not add the particles when we wish to express some sign of force, but begin simply from verbal forms.

It belongs to amplitude also, and makes the speech reputable and weighty, when someone does not introduce the matters by themselves and name them in terms of the subjects at hand, for example 'Callias appeared worth beholding because he was possessed by love of Autolycus', but also takes in from outside certain definite things for indefinite ones: 'Now all who are possessed by one of the gods seem worth beholding.' And if you had wished to pass quickly to the subject at hand and not to elevate the speech greatly, you would have said: 'but especially those possessed by love'; but as it is, it was elevated much more because the differences were taken up beforehand in between, before the subject at hand was brought in: 'but those [possessed] by other [gods] appear to look more fierce, to speak more fearsomely and to be more vehement'.

Keeping the figures in the nominative and not putting them in oblique cases is much more suited to history-writing, while putting them in oblique cases belongs to political speakers; for it has dignity and amplitude. If, then, you used the oblique case, you would speak thus: 'The horse race having ended'; while the nominative form is like this: 'When the horse race ended'; and this seems relaxed and slack. The political speaker would not have done it so, but more tautly: 'Since the horse race had ended.' And just as the political speaker is drawn together and has compressed his thoughts, so the simple one is laid back and stretched out.

This too is amplitude, as Socrates also said in the Symposium: 'It is clear in many other things too, and also in what the girl [does].' He spoke amply; and what is it that produced the amplitude? The taking in of the indefinite and the transition to something definite: 'in many other things too, but it is clear also in what the girl [does]'. And it is a Socratic and ancient manner to introduce something useful from every source, seeing that from the beginning, until they were found, there were discourses on virtue, and the greatest doctrine, that the virtue of men and of women is the same.
On sweetness.

We have said that sweetness of diction is supplied from comedy and from Plato and Xenophon; and simple writers also use poetic words, when they wish to confer bulk on the speech of their observations, and [words] from comedy. It is possible to begin from distributive particles and as if from an addition: 'and yet', 'and indeed', 'but then', 'but indeed'; for such things give simplicity to the speech.

And wherever you wish to produce sweetness, you will use such metaphors, transferring names that belong to some things onto others; and when you do not keep to the strictly denotative words, for example the word denoting the subject, 'they gave', and the word transferred by trope, 'and they honoured Chiron for his justice', instead of 'they gave'.

And by speaking of great things in a small way and of small things in a great way you will produce sweetness. We say, then, that naming small things in a great way gives sweetness to speech, and such a trope is most admirable, to speak of a war of a dog and a wild beast: 'First, the hounds of each breed must be [good], not just any that come to hand, so that they may be ready to wage war on the beast.'

He also produced wonderful sweetness in the Agesilaus, saying: 'Whenever he marched, he led the army so drawn up that they could best help one another'; then he added a comparison, as a simple man displaying sweetness together with dignity: 'but quietly, as the most modest maiden would walk forward'. The relaxation comes from the diminishing of the comparison and from its not being wholly alike; for how is a maiden like an army? Yet to say 'the modest maiden' would have had cheapness, while inverting it and making the accompanying [adjective] precede the person produced dignity with sweetness: 'as the most modest maiden'.

We spoke about sweetness in the preceding parts too, both what it achieves in political speech and again what in simple speech. Very nearly this virtue of sweetness belongs rather to the simple style.
On beauty.

Simple speech also takes on beauties from places, if it so happens, and from other accompanying things, for example when it speaks of a city great and prosperous, or of a river, where it flows from, how great its breadth: such things always add beauty to the speech. Now to go through in specific terms everything that belongs to a river or city or plain destroys simplicity, while [speaking] in general terms, as 'great and prosperous', preserves both the beauty and the plainness.
Juxtapositions of like things also make speech beautiful and pungent, as in the Anabasis, concerning Cyrus, he says: 'he set out prizes also for the cavalry units, for whichever rode best'.

And elaborations and figurings are invisible among simple writers. For this reason the ancients are worth much; for see how he figures it: 'and for the cavalry [units], whichever rode best'; for it was not the same to say 'for the horsemen', since it would quickly have made the speech combative, but 'for the cavalry units, whichever rode best'. So it has been figured from the plural to the singular and put in the nominative, and it is set beside a like phrase: 'for the cavalry units, whichever rode', and 'for the hoplite units, whichever was in the best bodily condition'.
On credibility.

The greatest thing in simple speech is that it should seem as true as possible, and that the things said should appear such that anyone would think them easy to conceive. This happens most when it takes its thought from the very matter being introduced, as in the Agesilaus he says that he wished to make war spending that man's [resources] rather than those of the Greeks. For taking this thought from what Agesilaus did (he was about to cross into Asia), through which he showed him to be prudent, he seemed to have spoken most truly about him.

It also makes speech true to introduce something that seems to be against you, admit it and let it stand without refuting it, for example: 'If any of you, seeing the enemy, has supposed them to be formidable, he seems to me to think rightly.' For so that Cyrus might seem to have spoken truly in the other things he went through with the soldiers, he not only did not refute this, which was against him, but even agreed with it.
And by introducing the things said in narratives, even if they are invented and small, they seem to be true; for he speaks of them as having happened.

And to say something briefly and to set many things alongside belongs to true force, for example: 'having called', then whom? 'Araspes'; then from where? 'a Mede'; then also for the sake of identification: 'who had been his friend from boyhood'; then another thing: 'to whom he gave the robe'.

These things, then, seem sufficient for advancing speech with force as well? But above all, when you do not accept as true something true that is said about you, that belongs to a simple man, as Socrates too says: 'You are always mocking us.' He has produced character through the modesty of his thought and through not boasting over the other man's praise, but treating it as mockery; for what the other said in earnest, he took as being mocked.
On arrangement.

Arrangement of speech in every case is the fitting order, the anticipation of what is to be said, the dependence of the thoughts on one another, and arguments that keep to the subject, and further the other principles that belong to simple arrangement. I mean this: if there is one heading, you must speak without anticipation of the reputable points on your own side, and then set down the anticipation, having first anticipated some of the opponent's reputable points against him; then in this way consider whether they also bring anything forward on our own behalf. If the points on the opponent's side are more numerous, you must consider the matter; for the method is the same. The main point is that you must show the enemies' points to be weak, and those on our own side to be far superior; for it is clear to everyone how it would come about, and it could not be otherwise.
On expression.

On expression I would say this much: use no noun or verb other than those from books, and you might put this simply: do not put everything into all the forms, but [also] each separately: what belongs to dignity, to simplicity, to emotion, to character, to anger. The parts of Demosthenes' speeches also contribute much to the form of expression, but Xenophon alone produces simplicity everywhere in his phrasing; for anger or emotion or wrath or sharpness, and all the other things that are agitated, belong to dignity or asperity, and to the change and urging of emotions, of the kind of thought Demosthenes has. The use of examples is Socratic, but something of this kind does not much suit political speech.

Sometimes Xenophon even introduces what he wants to say, before [saying] it, by means of the example itself; and his constructions are mostly without examples, as is clear in all his other works, but especially in the Memorabilia; for there, if you look closely, you can learn in what manner he has made Socrates discuss each subject and demonstrate each point, how he has been brought forward in this way.

The examples and the things set alongside, by which you demonstrate, must be similar to your subject and share something with the things being spoken of, either in kind, or in strength, or in time, or in their outcomes, or in their peculiarities, or in some other likeness. And this is fine in this form of speech and is what most produces simplicity; from it an interwoven abundance also arises, and the speech appears simple from the things brought round into it, both because what is said becomes more dignified and because it becomes more vivid through something else, which seems rather to be the work of conversation.
On arguments.

Of arguments, Demosthenes always, and those who have composed forensic speeches, make selections and distinctions, and mark out their force as they set down each one, reasonably doing this because their speech is combative, so that the hearers may learn their strength at once and be able to examine each point precisely.

But this does not seem to me to suit the simple style, if indeed the speech must appear as free from artifice as possible, simple and pure. Xenophon sets down each of his thoughts bare and separately, as in the Agesilaus, each by itself, so that one might even think the thoughts had been thrown down at random; yet they have not been thrown down, but each is brought forward with carefulness, though stripped of minute examination, addition, transposition, interchange and everything of that kind, and such things appear simple. Hence there are many continuous separations, and the beginnings of the thoughts are no longer united but complete in themselves; further, the things said appear very much as one thing after another, and the work is not like a woven fabric, but as if gathered comma by comma in the form of conversation.

This has made what is said seem to be a narration of a good man's deeds; but it does not, in my view, suit every simple speech wholly and in every case, and you must have learned this, if anything else, as a peculiarity of Xenophon; for this, I think, is what most makes speech simple.
On the beginning.

Come then, let us learn also about the beginning of a speech, the way in which Xenophon usually makes his beginnings. In all speeches alike one must prepare in advance something useful for the matter, and either resolve objections or establish them for oneself. In this respect, then, it is the same as in political speeches, but the peculiarities left to simple speeches are in treatment and delivery.

Political speakers take their beginnings both from the matters themselves and tending towards them, while Xenophon does not in every case make them tend towards them, and is accustomed not to take them from them, as in the Cyropaedia: 'The thought once occurred to us'; for he brought the speech forward not from Cyrus' deeds, but argumentatively from outside; hence as he proceeded he also made the amplification gradually from outside.

He has also used [beginnings] from the matters themselves in the Memorabilia, so that the speech seems downright forensic at the beginning of the first presentation of the matters, the thought not being complete: 'I have often wondered,' he says, 'by what arguments they persuaded the Athenians.'

This principle is in all the beginnings of his speeches: not to separate off the first thought by speaking as if introducing a second, but to subjoin at once what depends on the thought and to go on at length. A peculiarity is, without changing the quality of the thought, to introduce it first in general terms, as a political speaker would have done, elevating the speech with dignity, for example: 'The thought once occurred to us' what the nature of fine things happens to be, and then in this way the particular: 'how many democracies and how many tyrannies'. Another is not to use a negative figure, such as 'nothing is harder to persuade than human nature', but to examine it as humanly as possible with a question: 'The thought once occurred to us'; and to use not drawn-out but compact diction: 'The thought once occurred to us', [a mark] of simplicity.

At the end, let both the word and every sentence rest on a long [syllable]; the cola are judged by themselves, and let the speech be simple, as complete colon by colon, but showing in the form or quality of speech a certain density and a novel and simple interweaving. These effects are produced from a single word, for example 'the thought once occurred to us' instead of 'we once considered'. For sharp brevity produces simplicity, so that when the principle is changed, asperity or dignity happens to arise from simplicity; whence dignity comes to be something gentle.

In general, you must take your beginnings as the events happened, for example: 'To Darius and Parysatis are born two sons'; for here, even if the theme is great, the beginning is from certain bare facts.

The difference of subject matter makes a very great difference to the form of each kind of speech; for example, political speakers do not express doubt about reputable and well-known matters or persons, while the historical writer, by expressing doubt and hesitating, produces simplicity even with reputable matters.

The greatest thing of all in the simple style is to bring the matters forward bare and purely, and not to mark out their force in each case; for marking out belongs to the political man, when you add not only the matter but also its quality, as of something great if it is great, as of something terrible if it is terrible, things in which simplicity must have no share. For example, the simple writer says: 'He came forward and said this', but Demosthenes: 'He stood up and spoke words deserving, O Zeus and gods, many deaths.'

In many places Xenophon uses many forceful and Demosthenic [arguments] in his thoughts, and differs only in the treatment, as in the Anabasis, when speaking of certain reasonings about Tissaphernes, that he is not plotting against the Greeks: since the person is not credible as regards willing to plot, and he cannot establish it from his intention, he passes over and confirms it from his power: 'If, being able to do you harm, we do not do it, it is clear that we do not wish to either.' What then has made such forceful thoughts simple? The manner of treatment; for setting them side by side by possession and privation, and cutting the thoughts short, he says: 'Is it because you are in your own country and we in a foreign one, and because you are well supplied and we are in want?' So nothing else makes the thoughts unforced than the manner of delivery. So too he has done in the Agesilaus: since the speech was harsh in its thought, it was handled into simplicity by its delivery: 'if because he was exceedingly noble and good, he should for this reason not obtain even moderate praise.' But how do I mean this? That if the thought is of this kind, it makes the treatment harsh; for he did not say indignantly, as Demosthenes does: 'For it would be terrible if the letters sent by Philip...' Some usages are peculiar to simple speeches and you could in no way transfer them to a political speech, as here too: 'he was an exceedingly good man'.

In general, wherever he has stated many matters, unconnected, in the smallest space and has completed the thought, he has spoken with good rhythm, for example: 'When she stood up, all the women around her stood up with her.' Nor should one take in many matters in the simple style, as Demosthenes did: 'For if, when we came back after helping the Euboeans...', but [only] in a few, so that the speech may be as easy as possible for you to follow.

Using words in an unemphatic way produces cheapness. So the simple style is in danger of falling into cheapness, since it comes very close to it through using such words too. One can, then, escape and avoid cheapness by setting words of equal force side by side, for example: 'When Darius was ill and suspected the end of his life.' Using metaphorically words that properly belong to other things also belongs to simple writers, for example: 'He made many lovers of his own friendship', and again, 'the followers of the Greeks'; for he did not hesitate to call the last of the Greeks 'followers'. So does [repeating] the same word: 'They persuaded, we were persuaded.' So does cutting the thoughts short: 'We sent envoys.' For bringing things forward unconnected with one another makes the speech simple and displays a certain character, as of one telling things that happened quickly. Whatever names of places and spots are suitable in the simple style should be chosen, and further those that have less force and are less highly esteemed, such as gymnasia and hippodromes; and when you also set alongside them, choosing your words, 'gymnasia of men exercising', 'hippodromes of horsemen riding', all this belongs to simplicity. In the simple style words should also be brought forward not for one thing only, but should signify two or three; for example, since 'going away' has several kinds, all of these must be considered: for it includes both near and far, both on land and at sea, and having and causing trouble, and in short there are countless things it signifies. Words of the kind with which one can speak of barley, meal and oil seem rather to produce simplicity in a speech; for the speech is then about less reputable things. A political man would hesitate to approach such words; and wherever he does approach them, one should be well aware that he will bring them in either for vividness or so that character may arise in the speech. But the rhythm, being different, rescues the matters, and the unlikeness to the political style no longer lies in the thoughts but in the delivery; for what is political in a finished and complete way should be such both in thought and in delivery. Sometimes, however, the thought is simple but the delivery political, as Demosthenes does in the speech Against Callicles: 'that barley got wet, and they saw it being dried, not even three medimni, and of meal about half a medimnus; and of oil, he claims, a jar was tipped over, but it suffered no harm at all.' And this too is done with solemnity, since the proper word itself, if said, risks producing cheapness, as if you were to say 'but it was not spilled'; here instead of the proper and specific word he changed to the generic and said 'but it suffered no harm at all.' Linking things together by means of the same words seems to belong to the simple style, but it slackens the tension of the political style, as Demosthenes does in the speech On the False Embassy: 'For who does not know that by the Phocian war and by the Phocians being masters of Pylae...'; this safety arising from the place and the circumstances, however, he added in exclamatory fashion, as a completion.

Stating one's opinion in advance also belongs to simplicity, for example 'knowing well', 'thinking', 'believing'. It is also fine to suggest the thoughts and introduce them as if from the opinion of others. Xenophon uses this especially in the Education [of Cyrus], saying on each occasion: 'If any of you thinks this...'

Not being astonished at what one might be astonished at, and not marvelling at what deserves marvel, but simply telling what happened without marking anything from oneself: this too belongs to simplicity.

Beginning from the nominative case makes the speech simple, and so does breaking up the thoughts into commas. Simple writers often also use ideas brought in from outside beside the subject matter, for example: 'We have never perceived herds combining against the herdsman.' Political speakers too use ideas from outside, such as histories or examples, but they prepare for them with announcements or statements of cause.

Alternations also suit the simple style, for example 'he thinks, not thinking', and beginning with the same words belongs to simplicity. It also belongs to simplicity to use not harsh words but subdued ones. For it belongs to asperity to say 'this in private, that in public', but the simple writer says 'at home and at the altars'. So does using prepositions such as these: 'it had been noised abroad' is simple.

Optatives also seem to belong rather to simplicity, as 'that he was worthy', 'if they were pious', 'as Socrates would say', and the like; and in the Anabasis: 'that they were capable of fighting', and what follows in the same figure, 'and that they were well disposed to him'. Optatives make the speech pure.

Not quickening the tension of the delivery, but slowing it and proceeding at leisure, belongs to simplicity, for example: 'But indeed no one could blame them for this either.' And as for outcomes, political speakers are accustomed rather to examine them according to the outcomes of absurdities, and this produces asperity for them, but simple writers rather according to the results of good things, for example: 'For this belonged to no other empire...'

Not straining too hard either in matters or in thoughts belongs to simplicity, and so do transitions such as 'but indeed', 'as indeed'. Not using one's own judgement when something is worthy of praise, but the common one, is very simple, for example: 'At once the many admired [him].' Here there is also another principle, not to say by hyperbole 'all admired', but in a subdued way 'the many admired'. It is also peculiar to simple writers to leave out the stronger supporting points and state the weaker ones, for example: 'One must have one's hopes of safety in being conscious of no impiety towards the gods and no injustice towards men.'

Placing words side by side and linked with one another, receiving no elaboration, belongs to simplicity, for example: 'both to Ionians and Aeolians and Hellespontines'. So does not avoiding words that have less force and are less highly esteemed, but saying both 'market' and 'in the market', and by kind 'smiths', 'shoemakers', and such things belong to simplicity. Often, when the difference is greater, you also link in this way: 'Some there are now who have even revolted'; and sometimes you said the thing alone and bare, sometimes you added the cause, for example: 'longing for freedom'. Using inquiring forms instead of demonstratives belongs to simplicity; for example, a demonstrative having vividness: 'For he, ruling very many cities on the mainland, and ruling islands too...' But vividness sometimes arises in simplicity as well, for example: 'Philammon, not that [he was weaker than] Glaucus of Carystus...'

It is also simple to establish not, as in a proposition, that something is honourable, but, as in a comparison, that it is more honourable than another honourable thing. So is, having said something by negation, to state the hyperbole in place of the denial, for example: 'not even if I were going to...' And to state, instead of the consequent, its opposite by refutation is simpler and more careful, for example here: 'he took care', whose consequent was 'he did not neglect'.

Asyndeta also belong to the simple style; for they break up the rhythm. This is contrary to the political style but suits the simple, for example: 'Athenians, Thebans, Argives, Corinthians'. It is also simple not to speak collectively; for to speak collectively is to say 'the Persians', but partially 'the [affairs] of the Persians'.

[Speaking about matters while relying on the opinions of others also belongs to the simple style, for example: 'since they had quarrelled'. But when you say 'but since they quarrelled', it makes the speech harsh.] Using the same word often while changing its cases, turning it back, belongs to simplicity. Of the same kind is this: not concealing either the matter or the name, nor speaking obscurely, for example: 'He was saying to Cyrus'. It is characteristic of historical writing, if a complete statement is needed, to add after the specific names an indefinite one as well, for example: 'to Gorgias and Prodicus and many others'. When the thought is completed by a single completing word and comes to rest at the end on one word, as here: 'As he was quite plainly annoyed if they would not follow, they went along with [him]', it is characteristic of historical writing and of a speech that has character. Things said one by one, for example 'all bronze, all crimson', belong to simplicity; but saying them in the plural belongs to elaboration and dignity.

Connections are more a feature of combative speeches, but they may sometimes occur in the simple style too, when the beginning is compact because of the connection and what follows is loose, for example: 'he was burning and plundering'. The repetition of the connection also produces pungency: 'at the same time he was burning, and at the same time he was announcing it by proclamation', not 'he was proclaiming' or 'he was ordering it to be proclaimed'.

In the simple style it is enough to state not only the events themselves but also how they happened to occur, for example: 'Philip the jester, having knocked at the door'.
