The phrase 'having knocked (krousas) at the door' has been noted because the word used is not only kopsas but also krousas, though some do not think so; that it is good Greek, there is no need to dispute. But you, if you wanted to amplify the speech in the political manner, would have added to them their force as well: 'Philip was a jester, who suddenly appears; and when he found no one near him, he first decided to leap in, but then he thought it better to give a signal to someone else, and he went up and began to knock at the door.'

Saying some things about matters while relying on the opinions of others belongs to the simple style, for example: 'as it is said'. It is characteristic of a political speaker to introduce most things himself on his own authority; for example, Thucydides seems to have spoken simply in 'having quarrelled among themselves for many years, as it is said'; but if he says 'but since they quarrelled', it makes the speech harsh.

Some things are fine in the simple style but low in the political, for example 'living the life of hares'; for this is said in disparagement, yet it has its place, since speech proceeds one way in simplicity and another in cheapness. So whenever you wish to disparage something, bring it in breaking it up one item at a time, as Demosthenes does: 'leader and chief and ivy-bearer'. In carefulness and in dialogue it is fitting for simplicity of speech to be mixed with the beginnings of dignity. Ending on the same sound, though set apart so as not to spoil the speech, also produces simplicity.

Making fictive speeches is very fine in the simple style, and it has wonderful vividness. For example, if you wished to say it in fictive form: 'He himself came up and said that he had met them at the right moment', but Xenophon: 'I have met you at a good moment'; for breaking up and making fresh beginnings belongs to simplicity. In such cases, when you vary and, completing each thought, carry the speech on through many beginnings, it seems to belong to novelty and the more delicate form, as here: 'There was by the road a spring called the spring of Midas, the king of the Phrygians'; then another beginning: 'at this Midas hunted the satyr'; and another beginning: 'the manner of the hunting: he mixed it with wine'. Such beginnings, then, and continually putting the speech in the nominative in this way, belong to the more delicate form. It belongs to the more ancient manner to stretch out and go through the whole in a single course of speech: 'There was by the road a spring called the spring of Midas, the king of the Phrygians, at which Midas is said to have hunted the satyr; and the manner, how? By mixing it with wine'; for the speech is brought to a close from a single beginning to a single end. And this is of Xenophon's type. About obscure matters I have often said that one should speak as from hearsay. This also suits the simple style, for example 'it was said', and 'he was said to have given Cyrus much money'. About mythical matters, [one should say] not that it happened, but that it is said to have happened. We have said that novelties also belong to simplicity; so it is no bad thing to use an example here too, as Xenophon says in the Anabasis of Cyrus: 'he sacrificed the Lycaea'. This is very novel, a peculiar construction, 'he sacrificed the Lycaea'. For he has used the name of the festival as though it were the thing sacrificed, saying the event in terms of that in which it takes place and on account of which it takes place; for 'to sacrifice at the Lycaea' is the usual thing to say, but 'to sacrifice the Lycaea' is novel, as if you were to say 'he sacrificed the Panathenaea' and 'he sacrificed the Olympia'; the usual thing is to say also 'to sacrifice sacrifices'. [And this is usual to say.] It belongs to a worked-up speech to add details from places, where and near what and under what, as is also found in the Anabasis of Cyrus: 'There is also a palace of the Great King in Celaenae, fortified, at the springs of the river Marsyas, below the acropolis.' Then the same resumption, so that there is another beginning: 'This river flows through the city too and falls into the river Maeander.' And again another famous thing from the place: 'Here Apollo is said to have flayed Marsyas, who had contended with him about skill.' As we said before, one must know this about myths, that they are introduced not as having happened but as said to have happened. Then one must also know this, that the ancient manner, even when it deals with very famous matters, does not have the same elaboration in itself, but is content to state the matters and the manner in which they were done, without elaborating them at all; for elaborating and lingering over them because they are famous is what draws the speech away from the ancient type. 'Here', he says, 'it is said'; he did not say, 'Here is Marsyas the piper, a Phrygian by race, who was moved to such pride'; for that becomes lingering and elaboration. And note this too: he reversed the order. For the first thing would have been to say that he contended, then that he was defeated, then what he suffered; but in such cases, when you reverse the order and put the last thing first, and then the things before it in sequence, you will give the speech speed and beauty, when, after it has said what he suffered, the speech seeks why he suffered it: 'having contended not about piping or music, but about skill'. And about the skin, another would have said that it hangs [there], but again that is juvenile; he says 'and hung up the skin in the cave from which the springs come'. Then, as necessary and not elaborated: 'and for this reason the river is called Marsyas'. See in this too the restraint of the ancients; for he did not tell the suffering for which he gave the name of Marsyas to the river, or the misfortune of the piper; Xenophon does none of these things, but this much alone suffices him: 'and for this reason the river is called Marsyas'. Then another beginning from something famous: 'Here Xerxes, when he was withdrawing from Greece after being defeated in the battle'. See the restraint here too: there is no Salamis here, no expedition and multitude of infantry and triremes, nor how he was defeated, nor how he fled, nor anything else, though so much attached to Xerxes, but merely 'when from Greece'. You have learned, then, how the ancients go through things and how great their restraint is in these matters.

Observe this above all in thoughts: that the completing words should be held in reserve and placed last, so that the speech may also have a share of solemnity. Note this too, that in the simple style, even if some of the matters are greater and more important and others lesser, they are accustomed always to put the lesser first, as here: though it was a great and famous thing that Cyrus gave so much money to Clearchus, he did not come to this at once but first spoke of his judgement: 'he admired him and gives him ten thousand darics'. The beginning is: 'Clearchus was a Lacedaemonian exile; having associated with him, Cyrus...' The expression has a wonderful force of character in not saying 'Cyrus, having tested him' or 'having perceived him to be of great worth and most skilled in generalship', but simply 'having associated with him'. And what follows next, so that the character might appear most clearly, runs thus: 'he admired him and gives him ten thousand darics'.

I have often said that things put in comparison belong to simplicity, for example: 'she loved Cyrus more than the reigning Artaxerxes'. So also this: 'so that they were friends to him rather than to the king'. Using less emphatic words and naming great things by lesser names also belongs to the form of simplicity. In the Anabasis, of Cyrus: 'and he took care of the barbarians with him'; small names for a great matter, for 'taking care' is proper to nothing but modest things, and one might say 'he takes care of a household', but it is less fitting to use such a word of an army. And in the Agesilaus: 'and he stayed there again, pleased with the deed'. For using less emphatic words and not saying 'being proud' or 'elated by the victory' but 'pleased with the deed' belongs to simplicity.

The change of tense also belongs to simplicity: for they define the past in terms of the present, for example 'and he sends for Cyrus from his province' instead of 'he sent for'; for the tense, once changed, produced the simplicity. For we must sometimes set out things that have happened as happening, for example 'he calls him into the house and converses with him', [presenting] what happened long ago as happening now, and there is novelty in such a thing.

If by comparative forms you take away from the magnitude, care is rather produced, as in the Agesilaus: 'The king of the Persians, considering Tissaphernes to be the cause of all these things, of his own affairs going badly, sent down Tithraustes and cuts off his head'; and 'cuts off his head' belongs to simplicity, while 'considering' contains a certain disposition of the underlying matters: for he did not say 'since the affairs of the barbarians had gone badly, and so great was the uproar and confusion, and they had been defeated in so many battles, and finally, shut in, they were being besieged', nothing of the sort, but brought out only 'considering', and not 'at once provoked by what had happened and at once judging', but 'considering'. And the comparison: 'after this the affairs of the barbarians became more dispirited'; and he did not say 'in terrible dispiritedness' but 'more dispirited'. And speaking partially, 'the affairs of the barbarians', and not 'the barbarians', this too belongs to simplicity, as in 'who, ruling very many cities on the mainland, and ruling islands too'.

Further, some words signify strongly, others less so: strongly, for example, 'he marched through', 'he drove out'; less so, 'he journeyed', as also of Agesilaus: 'On the next day, crossing the Achaean mountains of Phthia, he journeyed through all the rest through friendly [territory] to the borders of the Boeotians.' Novelty too has simplicity: for he transferred what belongs to the person to the place; for instead of saying 'through the [land] of the friends' he says 'through friendly [territory]', and instead of 'through the [land] of the allies', 'through allied [territory]'. The simple writers also use 'here' (ἐνταῦθα) in varied ways: for it signifies both place and time, and 'here' takes hold of the place, while the separation is simple, for it sets the thought apart from what precedes. And sometimes one uses the complete demonstrative 'here indeed' (ἐνταῦθα δή), sometimes the defective 'there indeed' (ἔνθα δή).

Concerning the trope as it is found among the prose-writing men, one need know this much: that tropes should not be taken from great or solemn things, but rather from meaner or more common ones, as in the Symposium: 'with these men here, cleansed out in their souls'; for the word 'cleansed out', having its trope from utensils or vessels, transferred from more common things to more solemn ones, to men and to the soul of men, has made the trope not pure, but guarded and suited to prose. And such tropes are more customary in simplicity, for example 'and the [land], inhabited and sown, provides perpetual nourishment'. Such a figure belongs very much to the encomiastic form.

Matters of order must be so arranged as seems to suit each case: for in histories the facts themselves determine the order of what is said, but in precepts, teachings and memoirs, [it is] as one wishes.

Having observed these things carefully, then, and trained yourself in them, you will produce care where there is dignity and dignity out of care, and simplicity will be such as to have in everything the force of these principles. These things, then, have been adequately shown to you concerning what we proposed: all the principles for each kind of expression, concerning character, beginnings of speech, treatment of thoughts, and sweetness of expression, and again simplicity of expression, narrations and mythical modes, and concerning beauty in speech; these too have each been discussed.
